title: docs(design-note): how a Trust Ceremony works — the six decisions ADR 0001 deferred (#194)
body:
docs(design-note): how a Trust Ceremony works — the six decisions ADR 0001 deferred (#194)

* docs(design-note): how a Trust Ceremony works — the six decisions ADR 0001 deferred

ADR 0001 named the layer and deferred its design. This takes those six
decisions: the threading model, the definition format, evidence levels and who
issues a receipt, abort semantics, aggregate side-effect/exposure composition,
and the discovery extension.

The load-bearing proposals:

- One signed top-level 'ceremony' member (definition, enactment, step, prev).
  Not parentThreadId, which carries no normative semantics, records one level
  where ceremonies nest, and points at a threadId that is not required to be
  unique. Not payload (every task schema would have to opt in) and not ext
  (§4.5.1 item 6 forbids cross-specification semantics, so no standard ceremony
  could exist). Top-level also means signed, which is what prevents a step being
  lifted into another enactment or reinterpreted under another definition.

- Four evidence levels — collected, chained, receipt, countersigned — declared
  per definition on the same pattern the framework already uses for
  proofRequirement, sideEffects and exposure. A receipt attests completeness and
  ordering only, never content, so the recorder is not a trusted third party;
  receipt implies chained, because without the chain the ordering claim rests on
  nothing.

- Ceremony membership is a claim, not a fact: a consumer MUST NOT grant
  authority on the basis of membership alone, or the member becomes a
  confused-deputy vector.

- Aggregate exposure ships declared unsolved rather than as max() over the
  steps, which is wrong whenever correlation across differing audiences is
  itself the disclosure.

Deliberately excluded from the definition format: loops, timers, mapping, and
predicates over payload contents — the criterion being that a definition stays
readable in one sitting by the body that must approve it.

§14 records what is not true yet, including the untested assumption that
branching reduces to step optionality plus prev, and that nothing here has met
a wire.

Also points ADR 0001's Related row at this note, which it previously deferred to
by description only.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* docs(design-note): instrument VTC member onboarding, and standardise digests on multibase-multihash

Two additions, one of which falsified part of the note.

WORKED EXAMPLE (§13). VTC member onboarding is a real eight-step, four-role
flow built from shipped specs: join-requests/{manifest,submit,submit-receipt,
status,decide} then members/{solicit-vmc,request-vmc,vmc}. Instrumenting it:

- Confirms §1's claim rather than asserting it. solicit-vmc returns a threadId
  in its *payload* as the correlation handle across three party pairs, because
  the framework offers nowhere else to put it — and inherits exactly the
  weakness §5.1 identifies, since §4.9 does not require threadId to be unique.
  members/vmc's optional requestId carries the same load, for what the registry
  itself calls the 'join-ceremony close'.
- Exercises the partial order on the first flow tested: acknowledge and decide
  both depend only on apply, so a linear prev would have forced a false
  ordering.
- Validates step names over Type URIs: the retirement of join-requests/accept
  into members/vmc means one Type URI serves two steps whose meaning differs by
  context.

- FALSIFIES §6.2's blanket no-loops rule (§13.4). The deferred
  supplementary-evidence cycle is unbounded repetition. Amended to allow bounded
  repetition with a declared maximum, which keeps the one-sitting readability
  criterion; §6.2 now carries a forward pointer and §15 records it as tested-
  once-partly-failed rather than untested.

- Finds a gap in the VTC specs (§13.5): status can return deferred with needs,
  but no task supplies the evidence — submit takes no requestId and there is no
  supplement task, so deferred has no defined exit. Worth noting how it
  surfaced: authoring a definition is a reachability check over the registry,
  which is a stronger argument for the format than anything in §6.

- Adds a counter-example (§13.6): personhood, rotation and passkey enrolment are
  called ceremonies in shipped prose but need none of this layer. The framework
  sense is narrower than the colloquial one, and ADR 0001 §6 needs a row saying
  so.

DIGESTS (§7.7–7.8). Every digest here is now a multibase-encoded multihash over
the RFC 8785 (JCS) canonicalization, carried as digestMultibase — the W3C VCDM
2.0 property, matching what vta/credentials/issue already does for policyHash
and what did:webvh uses for SCIDs. Multihash carries the algorithm in-band, so
the sibling design note's 'state the aspiration, do not claim the capability'
warning about hard-coded SHA-256 does not apply here. prev entries carry
{id, digestMultibase} so a verifier can locate what it is checking.

§7.8 records the survey: 18 digest fields across four incompatible conventions,
with audit and provision/integration on hex. Converging them is staged as 1a
rather than done here — moving off hex is a breaking change needing new version
folders under §5.2. did:webvh SCIDs and nextKeyHashes are excluded as
externally-owned values per §4.10 item 5.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* docs(design-note): fix four verification-breaking defects found by adversarial re-read

An adversarial re-reading of the first draft found four security defects, each
of which independently breaks end-to-end verification. They are fixed in place
rather than listed as caveats, and §16 is new: it records what they were and why
they were missed.

1. The definition was referenced by MUTABLE URI. Whoever controlled
   trusttasks.org/ceremony/... controlled the completion rule, role list and
   evidence level — retroactively, for every enactment ever run. Adds a signed
   ceremony.definitionDigest so a step commits to the exact rules it ran under,
   which also disposes of definition-revised-mid-enactment.

2. The receipt was TRUNCATABLE. A chain catches an omitted step only via its
   successor, so dropping the trailing steps is invisible and any valid prefix
   passes as a complete enactment. Adds a signed terminal marker and moves
   completion evaluation to the verifier, which only works because the
   definition is now pinned — the two fixes are load-bearing on each other.

3. prev digests were UNSALTED. A decide payload is about one bit, so a party
   handed the digest can enumerate and confirm it. Salted per enactment.

4. Bounded repetition (§13.4) admitted REPLAY between rounds of the same step.
   Adds a signed round index.

Also resolves two internal inconsistencies and one omission: the evidence level
sat in the definition while §2 promised evidence-only adoption (§7.6 now splits
at collected/chained vs receipt/countersigned); the layer quietly weakened SPEC
§1's self-containment property (§6.3 states the cost honestly rather than
engineering it away); and completion rules could not express thresholds, which
is the ordinary currency of the governance domain this exists to serve (§6.1).

Adds the digest scope rule (over the predecessor INCLUDING its proof, with the
reasoning), key-rotation-mid-enactment resolution at issuedAt, and conformance
fixtures to §15.

Three mermaid diagrams where prose was doing badly: the VTC join sequence
showing three party pairs, the definition as a DAG showing the concurrency a
linear prev would have destroyed, and the truncation gap. First mermaid in the
repo; specs use ASCII, but these render on GitHub where design notes are read.

Marks Stage 1a done (#195) and updates §7.8, which described the inconsistency
that PR as now resolved.

THE PATTERN, recorded in §16 because it matters more than the fixes: findings 2
and 3 were already written down in this repo. audit/verify says a truncation to
a valid prefix is indistinguishable from a quiet period; task-consent's schema
says an unsalted digest over a low-entropy payload is a confirmation oracle. The
draft cited both as precedent, took the mechanism, and left the warning behind.
Borrowing a mechanism means inheriting its documented weaknesses.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* docs(design-note): resolve seven open items, and nest ceremonies to arbitrary depth

Works through §15 and closes seven of the nine open items, moving each into the
body rather than leaving it listed as unknown.

- Partial-order verification (§7.9, new). The first draft called this a
  graph-matching problem and left it unspecified, which overstated it badly:
  step is a LABEL, so a verifier looks documents up by name rather than
  searching for a matching subgraph. Linear in the number of documents. Written
  out as eight steps, because the wrong intuition here would justify a far more
  complicated design than the problem needs.

- Recorder availability (§7.4). A definition MAY name several recorders, any of
  which may issue. The first draft posed a false dilemma between trusting one
  recorder and paying for countersigned; plain redundancy costs nothing, since
  integrity rests on the terminal marker and the pinned definition rather than
  on who issued. countersigned answers recorder MISBEHAVIOUR, which is a
  different problem from recorder ABSENCE.

- Timeout (§9). Definition declares maxDuration; the clock starts at the
  issuedAt of the step whose prev is empty, so the deadline is derived rather
  than asserted by any party; a step MUST NOT carry an expiresAt beyond it, or a
  stale approval outlives the flow and replays into a closed enactment; late
  steps are rejected with the existing expired error code.

- Enactment correlation (§10). Now solvable rather than merely named:
  enactmentPrivacy: blinded carries H(enactment || stepSalt) per step, with the
  receipt revealing salts. Defaults OFF, because participants are normally meant
  to know they share a flow.

- Aggregate exposure (§11). 'Unsolved' was giving up early. max() is not the
  value but is a sound LOWER BOUND, so the definition declares its aggregate and
  the build enforces declared >= max(steps). Author judgment where judgment is
  needed; machine-checked against understatement, which is the failure mode that
  matters. What stays underivable is the true value, and why: correlation across
  disjoint audiences is itself a disclosure.

- Nesting (§5). Adds ceremony.parentEnactment, taking §4.9.2's posture exactly —
  one level, navigation only, never self-referential.

- The branching assumption (§15). Re-tested against four more flows: task-consent
  (request -> N x decision -> granted), credential-exchange issuance and
  presentation, and credential-exchange/pending. Holds across five flows now. The
  only construct any needed beyond the amended rule was the threshold — and
  task-consent's payload.minApprovals is REQUIRED and shipped, so thresholds are
  table stakes rather than a nice-to-have. Notably task-consent is NOT a loop: N
  approvers each perform one decision, which is a threshold over a step set.

COMPOSITION (§6.5, new). A step may name a ceremony instead of a Trust Task, so
a large flow is assembled from parts designed, reviewed and versioned
independently — and §6.2's one-sitting criterion survives growth, because a
reader takes one level at a time. Depth is unlimited by design.

The receipt is what makes the recursion need no new machinery: a task step
completes when its documents exist, a ceremony step completes when its
sub-enactment satisfies its own completion rule, and the artifact saying so is
the child's receipt — itself a Trust Task document, so it digests and chains
like any other step. One level down it is evidence about a flow; one level up it
is a step. parentEnactment pointers form a chain, so one level per document
still reaches any depth — which is why one level suffices here where §4.9.2
judged it insufficient for parentThreadId: threads have no addressable artifact,
enactments have receipts.

Four rules fall out, all checkable at publication: definitions MUST be acyclic;
a child's evidence level MUST be >= its parent's; a child's deadline MUST fall
within its parent's; role mapping MUST be explicit. Exposure floors compose
recursively.

The cost is stated rather than engineered away: depth multiplies the §6.3
self-containment problem, and a verifier SHOULD declare a maximum depth it will
resolve, as SPEC §10.2/§10.3 already do for parser and schema limits.

Two items remain open, both work rather than unknowns: the definition schema
(now unblocked — thresholds, repetition and composition are all settled) and
conformance fixtures. Composition itself is designed but untried, and §15 names
the test: VTC onboarding containing a webvh witnessing ceremony.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(ceremonies): definition meta-schema, first definition, and publication checks

Closes the two remaining items from the design note's §15 by building them,
and the composition test that preceded the schema found four things.

WHAT LANDS

- ceremonies/ceremony.meta.schema.json — the definition format, mirroring
  specs/spec.meta.schema.json. Roles with cardinality, steps of kind task or
  ceremony, prev as a set, bounded repetition, evidence level with plural
  recorders, maxDuration, enactmentPrivacy, and a closed completion-predicate
  DSL.
- ceremonies/vtc/member-onboarding/0.1/ceremony.json — the first definition,
  built only from Type URIs that exist in the registry today.
- scripts/validate-ceremonies.mjs — publication-time checks JSON Schema cannot
  express, plus a --test mode.
- ceremonies/ceremony.invalid-examples.json — 14 fixtures, each of which MUST be
  rejected, plus a control asserting the unmutated base passes.

npm run validate-ceremonies / npm run test-ceremonies. 14/14 rejected.

WHAT THE COMPOSITION TEST FOUND

Working VTC onboarding nested with webvh witnessing on paper, before writing the
schema:

1. The threshold construct was modelled wrongly, and against evidence already
   cited. §15 claimed task-consent's minApprovals was a threshold over distinct
   named steps. It is not: N approvers each perform ONE step, and the approvers
   are not known when the definition is written. That needs a threshold over the
   INSTANCES of one step, which the design did not have. Both shapes now exist —
   `of` over distinct steps, `ofStep` over instances of a perRole step — and the
   second is the more common governance shape.

2. Fan-out to a runtime-determined party set was inexpressible. Steps assumed one
   issuer. A witness set signing, or an approver set deciding, needs one instance
   per bound VID. Added as multiplicity: perRole, discriminated on the wire by
   the signed issuer, so no new envelope field is needed and one participant's
   instance cannot be replayed as another's.

3. Roles needed cardinality. perRole and instance-thresholds both require a role
   that binds to a SET rather than a single VID.

4. A party essential to a ceremony's meaning may be party to none of its steps.
   The did:webvh witness oracle signs inside payload.witness and the hosting
   service verifies it; it exchanges no Trust Task document. Added as
   evidentiary: true, with the honest consequence recorded — a ceremony attests
   who exchanged documents, NOT who signed material inside a payload. A receipt
   cannot carry that claim, and the checker rejects an evidentiary role used as a
   step issuer or recipient.

Also worth recording: webvh witnessing turned out to be a poor nesting example,
because the inner thing is one task plus internal replication rather than a
ceremony. §13.6's rule holds — a two-step exchange needs none of this layer — so
the first real nested definition still awaits a genuine multi-party inner
ceremony.

ON THE COMPLETION PREDICATE

A closed set of combinators, not Rego, though the stack already embeds regorus
for policy. Rego answers a RUNTIME question (may this happen?); completion is an
EVIDENCE question settled at verification time, possibly years later, offline, by
a third party who must not have to execute anyone's code. Keeping it enumerable
is also what lets a governance body read every path as a checklist, which is the
§6.2 criterion the whole format exists to protect.

ON THE FIXTURES

A checker that has never been shown to fail is not evidence of anything, and
§7.8 found the registry's own example validation would not have caught a
comparable drift. The first run of these fixtures caught 0/12 — the harness was
resolving the wrong root, not the checks failing — which is exactly why the
control case asserting the unmutated base passes is now part of the suite.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* docs(design-note): fold in what building the schema found, and state that ceremonies are optional

Four corrections from writing ceremonies/ceremony.meta.schema.json and working a
nested definition against real specs, plus one gap a reader would hit immediately.

CORRECTIONS (§6.1, §6.1.1, §16 round two)

- The threshold construct was modelled wrongly, against evidence this note
  already cited. §15 called task-consent's minApprovals a threshold over
  distinct named steps. It is a threshold over the INSTANCES of one step, and
  which approvers act is not known when the definition is written. Both shapes
  are now described — `of` over distinct steps, `ofStep` over instances — and
  §15's bullet is corrected rather than left standing.

  Worth dwelling on: the evidence was in hand and the wrong conclusion was drawn
  from it in the same paragraph that recorded it. Citing a flow correctly is not
  modelling it correctly, and the error survived the adversarial re-read because
  that round was hunting security defects, not modelling ones.

- Fan-out to a runtime-determined party set was inexpressible; steps assumed one
  issuer. Now multiplicity: perRole, distinct from maxRounds — multiplicity
  varies the party, repetition varies the attempt.

- Roles had no cardinality, which both of the above require.

- New §6.1.1: a party can be essential to a ceremony's meaning and party to none
  of its steps — did:webvh's witness oracle signs inside payload.witness and
  exchanges no document. This changes what the layer can CLAIM: a ceremony
  attests who exchanged documents, never who signed material inside a payload,
  and a receipt cannot carry that claim.

- New §6.5.1: webvh witnessing turned out to be a poor inner ceremony — one task
  plus idempotent replication — so member-onboarding contains no kind: ceremony
  step and composition remains specified, checkable, and UNEXERCISED. Said where
  the reader meets composition, not only in §15.

OPTIONALITY (§2.1, new)

The note never answered whether this layer is optional for a Trust Task. It is,
in both directions, and the claim is precise: no specification ever changes,
because the member is on the envelope rather than in payload; a document without
it is conforming; and a consumer need never implement ceremonies at all.

Ignoring the member is ALWAYS safe, and by construction rather than luck —
because §10 forbids deriving authority from ceremony membership, there is
nothing a ceremony-aware consumer may do that an unaware one omits. A layer
whose neglect changed an access decision would be a security defect. Producers
opt in per document; consumers never have to.

Also notes that the 0.3 envelope schema already accepts the member
(additionalProperties: true, §4.2), so 0.4 adds the MEANING of the member, not
permission to send it.

PREAMBLE

No longer claims nothing is implemented — the definition format, a first
definition, publication checks and 14 fixtures now exist. It remains true that
nothing is on the wire, and §15 still says so.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* docs(design-note): Stage 0 is shipped, and drop a duplicated bullet

trust-task-next-step/0.1 merged as #196, so the note's four descriptions of it
as reserved-and-unspecified were stale: §2's concerns table, §3's inventory, §8
itself, and the §14 staging table.

§8 now records the two things building it settled that bear on the rest:

- A next step is a THIRD disposition rather than a variant of the other two. A
  success response and an error response both CLOSE the originating task; a next
  step leaves it open. That is now normative in SPEC §8.6 rather than only in the
  registry entry, because it is a framework rule about how the three replies
  relate.

- Its `expects` is a list of alternatives, never a conjunction — and that is
  where this layer's boundary got drawn in practice. A conjunction would have
  given a single reply ordering, optionality and completion, which is a flow
  definition and the exact material §6 keeps in a ceremony. Allowed to express
  'do all of these first', trust-task-next-step would have become a ceremony
  format by accretion, one field at a time, with none of §6.2's constraints on
  it.

Also corrects §15's honesty about implementation. Next-step is published and
generated into both libraries, but it is the coordination concern and carries
none of the evidence machinery — no digest, chaining, projection or composition
claim has been exercised between two parties, and none can be until the ceremony
envelope member exists. The bullet said 'no implementation exists', which is now
both wrong and too generous to the parts that matter.

Removes a duplicated 'No implementation exists' bullet left by an earlier edit,
and updates the preamble to reflect two revision rounds rather than one.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: feat(framework): specify trust-task-next-step, the third reply disposition
body:
SPEC §8.6 reserved `trust-task-next-step` and left its payload "out of scope for this revision". This publishes it.

It is **Stage 0** of the Trust Ceremonies staging in #194 — the cheapest useful increment of that layer, needing no envelope member, no definition format, and no framework version bump. It is independent of #194 and of ADR 0001 §5, and merges on its own.

## The point of the specification

A next step is a **third** disposition, and most of the design follows from it not being either of the other two:

| Reply | Means | The originating task is |
|---|---|---|
| `<type>#response` | The task completed | closed, successfully |
| `trust-task-error` | The task will not be performed | closed, unsuccessfully |
| `trust-task-next-step` | Understood, and **blocked** | **open** |

A blocked task reported as `taskFailed` with a helpful `message` is not the same thing. An error terminates the document under §8.4; only a next step tells a producer that continuing is expected of it.

## Design decisions worth reviewing

**`expects` is a list of alternatives, never a conjunction.** Satisfying any one entry unblocks the exchange. A recipient that needs two things done first names one and issues a further next step later.

That restraint is deliberate: expressing a conjunction here would give this response ordering, optionality and completion — which is a flow definition, and belongs to a ceremony. Keeping `expects` disjunctive is what stops this specification growing into one by accident.

**`continuation` is an enum, not a boolean.** `resubmit` (default) means the expected task is a prerequisite and the originating request is re-issued as a **new document with a fresh `id`** and the same `threadId` — which §8.4 distinguishes from a *retry*, since a retry is bit-for-bit identical and would carry a possibly-expired document. This is the shipped `task-consent/granted` pattern. `proceed` means the expected task is itself the continuation.

**`inResponseTo`** mirrors §8.2s member on the error payload, for the reason it was added there in #185: `threadId` correlates the exchange only for a party that already saw the request.

**No `response` anchor** — a producer answers by issuing a document of the *expected* type, not by responding to this one.

## Security

The asymmetry with an error response drives the whole section:

> A refusal that cannot be trusted is ignored. A redirection that cannot be trusted is **followed**.

So a consumer **MUST NOT** act on a next step whose origin it can authenticate neither in-band nor from the transport. `proof` is RECOMMENDED on a stronger rationale than for an error response — but not REQUIRED, because the document is consumed in-exchange and never retained by third parties, so §4.7.1s mandatory condition does not arise.

**It confers no authorization.** Suggesting a task does not make performing it approved. Every §7.3 item 13/14 gate and consent policy still applies, on the same advisory footing as a discovery response (§11.4). Also covered: downgrade suggestions, redirect loops (bounded producer-side as §10.2 does for parsers, rather than by a wire counter either party could reset), the discovery-style capability disclosure in `expects`, and `hint` as untrusted input.

## SPEC.md

Three prose corrections, in a Working Draft whose own Status section anticipates §8 evolving. §6.1s table and §1.1 goal 4 no longer call next-step merely reserved; §8.6 points at the registry entry as normative — the same relationship §11 has with `trust-task-discovery` — and records that `trust-task-ok` remains reserved. §8.6 also states the three-way distinction normatively, since that is a framework rule rather than one this spec can impose alone.

## Libraries

Additive, so a patch: `trust-tasks-rs` and `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.4.0 → **0.4.1**. No dependent crate needs a bump — their `"0.4"` requirement resolves and no existing type changed.

## One codegen fragility found

A **field-level** description containing blank lines generates a `/** */` doc comment whose continuation lines are indented four spaces inside the struct, which rustdoc reads as an indented code block and doctests as Rust. It failed `cargo test`. Type-level descriptions are unaffected, which is why `DigestMultibase` was fine in #195.

Worked around here by keeping the description single-paragraph. The codegen should probably escape this instead, and I can raise it separately — right now it is a trap for the next spec author who writes two paragraphs about a field.

## Verification

`npm run validate` — 289 specs (was 288), 54 shared schemas. `cargo check`/`test --workspace`, doctests, `cargo fmt`, and the TS build all pass; both bindings regenerated so the drift checks should be clean. 10 invalid examples confirm the schema rejects what it should.

title: docs(approvals): correct the plan for closing the REST gate
body:
Doc-only follow-up to #909, correcting guidance that PR merged.

## What was wrong

The design note told the next person to land the trigger collapse and the REST-gate unification as **one atomic change**, reasoning that deleting `resolve_step_up` without moving REST onto the shared gate leaves a release with REST un-gated.

The premise is right. The conclusion isn't: adding the shared gate to the REST handlers *while leaving* `RequireStepUp` in place is purely additive — REST is then gated by both the old floors and the PDP, so the deletion that follows removes nothing still carrying load.

- **Step 1** — add `approvals::gate()`, call it in the ~13 gated REST handlers, leave `RequireStepUp` alone. Closes the consent bypass on its own.
- **Step 2** — delete. Nothing to sequence inside it.

Two steps, no un-gated window, and the security fix ships without waiting on the retirement. Someone following the old note would have done more work for a worse outcome, which is why this is worth its own PR rather than being folded into the next one.

## Also recorded

Two shapes the refactor needs, both established by reading the code rather than sketching:

- `policy_gate` currently *decides* and *shapes a trust-task reject* in one pass — it threads `&TrustTask<Value>` down to nine `app_error_to_reject(doc, e)` sites plus several `reject_with(doc, …)` sites. A `GateReject` enum, with `consent_gate` / `require_step_up` / `initiate_self_step_up` taking `&Value` instead of the document, separates the two mechanically and leaves the decision logic untouched.
- **REST cannot currently carry the actionable payload.** `AppError::StepUpRequired(String)` renders `{error, message, requiredAcr}` with no `approveRequest`, and there is no consent variant at all. `AppError::ApprovalRequired { code, details }` fixes that, and is the same shape the typed SDK error in the final slice consumes — so both land on one variant rather than two.

The gate must be called **in-handler, after body parse**: the consent digest and the planner both need the payload, which an axum extractor does not have.

## Status line

Changed to say plainly that **a `requireConsent` rule is not enforced for REST callers until step 1 lands**. That is pre-existing behaviour, not introduced by #909, but the note previously buried it in a paragraph about sequencing.

No code changes; no crate versions touched, so no changelog fragment.

title: feat(approvals): one approval model, manageable at runtime
body:
## Why

An operator ran `pnm contexts create --admin-did …`. The context was created; the ACL grant behind it failed with `auth:step_up_required`. Three things about that failure were the actual problem:

1. The policy they were reading (`[[policy.require_consent]]`, naming a webvh task) was not the policy that fired (`[auth.step_up].floors`, naming `acl/grant`) — two config languages over two identifier spaces, answering the same question.
2. The reject carried an `approveRequest`, the one thing that could have unblocked them, and the SDK dropped it: only the *consent* arm has a typed error variant, so the step-up arm collapsed to an opaque string.
3. The floor could not be read back at all — step-up policy is REST-only in the SDK, and that VTA advertises no REST service. The only way to inspect the policy was to overwrite it.

None of those is a bug in isolation. Together they are a design that answers one question three ways: step-up floors (a closed list of 11 op-class slugs), `[[policy.require_consent]]` (task type URIs), and the messaging-consent registry — three approver registries, three ceremonies, three management surfaces, only one reachable at runtime.

This is the first half of collapsing them. It is **additive throughout**: nothing is retired, no path is un-gated.

## What's here

**One model** (`vta_sdk::approvals`) — a rule list keyed on task type URI (any URI, not the closed table), `requires: "reauth" | "consent"`, approver set, N-of-M threshold, `excludeRequester`, per-context scoping. Validation is **write-time**: an undefined or empty approver set, a threshold no set could meet, consent-only fields on a `reauth` rule, or two rules whose guards overlap are refused when written — not discovered by the first caller they block, which is exactly how the original `delegated` floor failed.

**Runtime PDP management** on the canonical `policy/{list,get,upsert,delete}` family. All four were already published upstream and none were served here: the VTA had *no* runtime policy surface, so changing what the PDP enforced meant editing `config.toml` and restarting. These ride `rpc_tt`, so they work over DIDComm and TSP — which is the point, given the VTA that prompted this advertises no REST.

**`pnm approvals {list,require,remove,approvers,explain}`** — plus `pnm policy {list,show,upsert,delete}` as the hand-authored-Rego escape hatch.

```
$ pnm approvals explain https://trusttasks.org/spec/vta/webvh/dids/update/1.0
  context: default
  requires: consent — 2 approval(s) from set `webvh-approvers`, requester excluded
  approvers: 1 member(s) — fewer than the 2 required, so this task can never run
```

## Two decisions worth reviewing

**The module is client-authored and byte-compared.** Canonical `policy/upsert` declares `module` `minLength: 1` and authoritative — the maintainer validates it, it does not invent it. So the caller generates the Rego from its rules and sends both, and the VTA re-derives from `ext["openvtc.approvals"]` and refuses the write unless the two are byte-identical. Trusting `module` and treating `ext` as decoration would mean the rules an operator reads back need not describe the Rego that decides; this is what makes the declarative view true rather than advisory. It also makes `synthesize_rego`'s output a wire compatibility surface.

**Config is a seed applied once**, not reconciled every boot like the consent policy it supersedes. Once rules are runtime-editable, re-reading the file on every boot means a restart weeks later — for an unrelated reason — silently reverts a change the operator made and verified. Pinned by a test.

## Not served, deliberately

- `policy/activate` / `policy/active` — they model an activation pointer this maintainer does not have (the active set is every enabled row in priority order).
- `policy/evaluate/0.3` — its `PolicyInput` still marks `site`, a vault-flow `SiteTarget`, as required, inherited from before 0.3 generalised the family. There is no honest `site` for "would `acl/grant` need approval here", and fabricating one puts invented data into a security decision's input. `vta-policy`'s own schema mirror already carries this as a known upstream wart. Until it is relaxed, `approvals explain` answers from the rules.

## What this exposes, and what comes next

The PDP gate runs **only** in the trust-task dispatcher. `routes/acl.rs::create_acl` and `routes/did_webvh.rs::update_did_handler` call their operations directly, so **a `requireConsent` rule is not enforced for a REST caller today**. That is pre-existing, not introduced here.

The follow-up retires `[auth.step_up]` and `[[policy.require_consent]]`, deletes the delegated step-up modes, and moves the gated REST handlers onto a shared gate. Those must land **together**: the only thing gating those REST routes is the `RequireStepUp` extractor, built on `resolve_step_up` — the function the retirement deletes. Splitting them leaves a release with REST un-gated. See `docs/05-design-notes/approvals-convergence.md`.

## Testing

Full workspace suite green. New coverage: deterministic-synthesis + injection-escaping tests; a regorus round-trip proving the generated module compiles *and* decides correctly (a module that failed to compile would be skipped at load and silently un-gate every task it named); byte-compare rejection; the reserved-id guards in both directions; super-admin gating; optimistic-concurrency conflict; seed-once (a runtime edit must survive a restart); unsatisfiable-seed boot refusal.

No new Trust Task URIs — the census and conformance harnesses pass without growing `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`. The conformance witnesses caught one real drift while being written: `policy/delete/0.1` names its response members `id` + `deletedAt`, not `deleted`.

title: feat(approvals): one approval model, manageable at runtime (#909)
body:
feat(approvals): one approval model, manageable at runtime (#909)

* feat(approvals): declarative approval rules + runtime policy/* management

The VTA answers "does this operation need an additional human decision?"
with three independent subsystems: `[auth.step_up]` floors keyed by a
closed list of eleven op-class slugs, `[[policy.require_consent]]` rules
keyed by task type URI, and the messaging-consent approver registry. Two
config languages over two identifier spaces, three approver registries,
three ceremonies — and only one of them reachable at runtime.

This is the first slice of collapsing them: the shared model, and the
surface that makes it editable without a config edit and a restart.

`vta_sdk::approvals` is one rule list keyed on task type URI (any URI,
not a closed op-class table), carrying `requires: reauth | consent`, the
approver set, threshold, `excludeRequester`, and per-context scoping,
plus the deterministic Rego synthesizer both the CLI and the VTA derive
from. Validation is write-time: an unknown or empty approver set, a
threshold no set could meet, a consent-only field on a `reauth` rule, or
two rules whose guards overlap are refused when an operator writes them
rather than discovered by the first caller they block — which is exactly
how a `delegated` floor with no approver used to fail.

The rules live in the `ext` of one reserved row in the policy keyspace,
managed through the canonical `policy/{list,get,upsert,delete}` family.
All four are already published upstream and none were served here: the
VTA had no runtime policy surface at all. They ride `rpc_tt`, so they
work over DIDComm and TSP, not only REST — the step-up policy surface
this begins to replace was REST-only in the SDK, so an operator on a
mediator-only VTA could not read the policy blocking them.

Canonical `policy/upsert` treats `module` as client-authored and
authoritative (`minLength: 1`), so the VTA must not synthesize over it.
Instead the caller generates the Rego from its rules and sends both, and
the VTA re-derives from `ext["openvtc.approvals"]` and byte-compares,
refusing a mismatch. The rules an operator reads back are therefore
guaranteed to describe the policy that actually decides, rather than
being advisory decoration next to Rego that might say something else.

`policy/activate` and `policy/active` are not served: they model an
activation pointer this maintainer does not have (the active set is
every enabled row in priority order). `policy/evaluate/0.3` is not
served either — its `PolicyInput` still marks `site`, a vault-flow
`SiteTarget`, as required, and there is no honest `site` for "would
`acl/grant` need approval here". Relaxing that upstream is the
prerequisite; until then `approvals explain` will answer from the rules.

No new Trust Task URIs, so the census and conformance harnesses pass
without growing `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`. The conformance witnesses
caught one real drift while being written: `policy/delete/0.1` names its
response members `id` + `deletedAt`, not `deleted`.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(approvals): manage approval requirements at runtime from PNM

Adds the operator surface over the declarative model: `pnm approvals`
lists the rules and approver sets, sets or removes a requirement, edits
the sets, and explains what a given task actually needs. Every command
is a read-modify-write of the one reserved policy row through
`policy/{get,upsert}`, carrying `expectedVersion` so two operators
editing at once collide rather than silently overwrite one another.

`explain` is the command this whole arc came from. A `pnm contexts
create` failed with `auth:step_up_required`, and the policy the operator
was reading was not the policy that fired — nothing on the VTA could say
"this task requires re-authentication, here is the rule". Now something
can, and when a rule is unsatisfiable (approver set undefined, or smaller
than the threshold) it says that outright instead of leaving it to be
discovered by the next request the rule blocks.

There is deliberately no `--module` escape hatch on this surface. The
CLI generates the Rego from the rules and the VTA re-derives and
byte-compares; a declarative row whose Rego disagreed with its rules
would make everything `approvals list` prints advisory rather than true.
Hand-authored Rego belongs to `pnm policy upsert`.

`[policy.approvals]` and `[policy.approver_sets]` become a seed applied
once, when the VTA boots without a declarative row — the bring-up path
for a fresh or IaC-provisioned agent. This is deliberately not the
reconcile-every-boot behaviour of the consent policy it supersedes. Once
the rules are editable at runtime, re-reading the file on every boot
means a restart weeks later, for an unrelated reason, silently reverts a
change the operator made and verified. A security control that quietly
undoes itself is worse than one that is awkward to change. A test pins
it: a runtime edit must survive a restart against the same config.

The consent gate now resolves approver sets from the row first and falls
back to config, so `approvals approvers add` takes effect without a
restart while a VTA whose sets are still in config keeps working.

The declarative row sits at priority 200, above the legacy
config-synthesized consent row at 100. A task named by both would
otherwise tie, and `decide()` breaks ties by keyspace iteration order —
so which requirement applied would have depended on disk layout.

Additive throughout: nothing is retired and no path is un-gated, so this
lands ahead of the trigger collapse rather than waiting on it.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(approvals): operator guide + convergence design note

Documents the surface `pnm approvals` now exposes, and records why the
VTA has one approval model instead of three — including what is still
pending and the coupling that constrains it.

Also stops a negative test fixture from tripping vtc-service's registry
census. The scanner treats any complete, version-terminated
`trusttasks.org/spec/…` literal under a binding site as a claim that the
registry serves that task, which is the right rule; it just cannot tell
a deliberately-malformed fixture from a real binding. Assembling that
one string at runtime keeps the test's coverage and leaves the guard as
strict as it was.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* chore(changelog): consolidate the approvals fragments onto #909

The two fragments were written assuming this would land as two PRs. It is
one, so there is no #910 for the second to name.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(cli): fold the policy-list NAME header into the format string

`cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings` rejects a trailing literal
argument (print_literal). Both the Clippy job and the feature-combos
"vta-service rest only" step failed on it — the latter because
vta-service depends on vta-cli-common, so the same lint surfaces twice.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

title: chore(specs): converge digest fields on multibase-multihash, and release 0.4.0
body:
Stage 1a from the Trust Ceremonies design note (#194 §7.8), which found the registry carrying **four incompatible digest conventions across 18 fields**.

| Convention | Fields | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Multibase-multihash over JCS — correct | 2 | `vta/credentials/issue` `policyHash` |
| "Multihash", encoding unstated | 4 | `chat/message`, `consent/request`, `policy/_shared/0.3` |
| Lowercase hex, SHA-256 hard-coded | 2 | `provision/integration` (`^[0-9a-f]{64}$`) |
| Unspecified entirely | 6 | `audit/_shared` `prevHash`/`entryHash`, `task-consent/*` `payloadDigest` |

A digest with no declared encoding is not interoperable; one with no declared canonicalization is not reproducible. Both defects were present.

## The definition

Adds `$defs/DigestMultibase` to a new `specs/_framework/0.3/framework.schema.json` — additive over 0.2, which is carried forward unchanged. It is the **W3C VCDM 2.0 `digestMultibase` encoding**, already used by `vta/credentials/issue` for `policyHash` and by `did:webvh` for its SCIDs and entry hashes. The algorithm now travels in the multihash instead of being fixed by the schema, so changing it no longer needs a schema revision.

It constrains the **encoding only**. What each digest is computed over is stated per field, because it differs legitimately — RFC 8785 (JCS) canonicalization for JSON documents, raw bytes for opaque artifacts.

## Done in place, per §5.2

Every affected artifact is `draft`, and §5.2's draft rule makes editorial/re-pinning changes in-place errata that **MUST NOT** mint a new version — explicitly taking precedence over §6.6's version-coupling. So: `audit/_shared`, `audit/verify`, `chat/message` (×2), `consent/request`, `policy/_shared/0.3`, `task-consent/{request,decision,granted}`.

Example digests in prose and invalid-examples moved from 64-char hex to multibase in the same pass. Worth flagging: **the build validates fenced examples against the envelope schema but not against payload schemas**, so those had drifted silently and validation stayed green throughout. That is a gap worth closing separately.

## Two deliberate exclusions

**`provision/integration` `summary.digest` is out.** It is not a Trust Task digest — it belongs to the OpenPGP-style sealed-bundle armor, which carries its own `Digest-Algo: sha-256` header beside a hex `Bundle-Id` and `bundleIdHex`. Converting one field of that format in isolation makes it *less* internally consistent. I applied the change, saw the surrounding format, and reverted it.

**`did:webvh` `scid` / `new_scid` / `newScid` / `nextKeyHashes` are out** as externally-owned values under §4.10 item 5. Their format belongs to the DID method.

## Library impact — this is a workspace event

Codegen emits `DigestMultibase` as a **validating newtype**, so affected payload members change from `String` and a raw hex digest that used to parse now fails at the boundary. Better — the encoding is type-enforced — and breaking.

Per `CLAUDE.md` that is a leading-component bump. And because `trust-tasks-rs` types cross every binding's public API, a graph mixing 0.3 with 0.4 will not type-check, so the dependents bump too even though none of them touch the changed specs:

| Crate | Version |
|---|---|
| `trust-tasks-rs`, `-https`, `-didcomm`, `-proof`, `-tsp` | 0.3.0 → **0.4.0** |
| `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` | 0.1.0 → **0.2.0** |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.2.0 → **0.3.0** |
| `@openvtc/trust-tasks` | 0.3.0 → **0.4.0** |

All six `trust-tasks-rs` requirements moved to `0.4`. Merging releases all of them via `publish.yml`.

## Verification

- `npm run validate` — 288 specs, 54 shared schemas (was 53)
- `cargo check --workspace`, `cargo test --workspace` — pass
- `cargo fmt --all` applied; Rust and TS bindings regenerated, so both drift checks should be clean
- `trust-tasks-ts` builds at 0.4.0

## Review note

This touches five spec namespaces plus the libraries, so CODEOWNERS will want several approvals. It cannot usefully be split: the drift checks require bindings to match specs in the same commit, and the version bumps are forced by the API break.

title: docs(adr): name the multi-task flow layer "Trust Ceremony" (ADR 0001)
body:
Trust Tasks works well where an interaction is one task and one response — most of the registry today. Interactions are now appearing that are not that shape: governance decisions requiring several endorsements, onboarding spanning a witness and a registry, credential exchanges with a consent step in the middle. These are built as several bilateral tasks correlated by `threadId`, with the knowledge of how they compose held in application code at each party.

SPEC §2 already settles the mechanism ("multiple bilateral *Trust Tasks* linked by `threadId`"). What is missing is a **name, a definition format, and an evidence artifact** for the collection.

**This PR adds only the ADR.** It decides a name and a vocabulary; it does not decide the design of the layer, which is deferred to a design note.

## Decision

**Trust Ceremony**, with a three-part vocabulary — **Ceremony** (the definition), **Enactment** (one run), **Ceremony receipt** (the evidence). Plus two namespace reservations: extending §6.1 to `^trust-(task|ceremony)($|-|/)`, and a `/ceremony/` subtree disjoint from `/spec/` and `/binding/` on the §9.3 pattern.

## Why record the name before the design

Two reasons, both in §8 of the ADR:

- **The name is load-bearing on the design.** The primary risk to this layer is not the data model — it is feature creep in the definition format (loops, timers, gateways) until it is no longer readable by the governance body that has to approve it. A name that implies limited scope is the cheapest available defence, and one that does not — *workflow*, *orchestration*, *flow* — invites exactly what we want to refuse.
- **Two consequences are expensive to reverse.** `trust-ceremony-*` is registrable by any contributor under the current §6.1 reservation. And if the layer contributes a top-level envelope member in framework 0.4, it is spelled `ceremony` or `choreography`; renaming it later is a leading-component bump across `trust-tasks-rs` and the six crates pinning `trust-tasks-rs = "0.3"`.

## Rejected options are on the record

Choreography, dance, rite, procedure, assembly, flow, sequence, saga, session, score — with reasoning, so review does not relitigate them from scratch. Two worth calling out:

- **Choreography** was the strongest alternative and is the technically more precise word. Rejected on the WS-CDL association, on carrying no implication of limited scope, and on speaking only to coordination — not humans, not evidence. The ADR recommends borrowing its machinery (endpoint projection, well-formedness checking) without its name.
- **Score** is recorded as a trap. The musical metaphor is apt and will be proposed; "Trust Score" collides with credit and reputation scoring.

## One sub-decision left open

The split vocabulary — **Choreography** (definition) → **Ceremony** (enactment) → **Receipt** — is arguably more precise than the single name, and dissolves the VTC question with no retconning. It costs two nouns and leaves no single name for the layer. §5 records it as live; it should be settled before 0.4.

## On `vtc/ceremonies/*`

Reuse of the word is deliberate and agreed. §6 carries a disambiguation table (scope, audience, identifier, what each produces) and requires it wherever both senses appear. The upgrade path needs no rename.

## Notes for review

- Establishes `docs/adr/` as the home for decision records; `docs/design-notes/` is unchanged.
- Docs-only. `npm run validate` passes — 288 specs, 405 example documents; the three `vta/did-templates` warnings are pre-existing and untouched.
- Collision counts in §4 are literal-substring matches across `SPEC.md`, `specs/` and `bindings/`, taken 2026-08-09.
- The first increment of the layer — specifying the already-reserved `trust-task-next-step` (§8.6) — needs neither reservation nor envelope member, so it is unblocked by this ADR either way.

title: chore: update every dependency to its latest release
body:
`cargo update` across the whole graph, plus the manifest bumps needed to cross a major boundary.

| Crate | From | To |
|---|---|---|
| `vta-sdk` | 0.20.24 | 0.21.7 |
| `affinidi-messaging-sdk` | 0.18.60 | 0.19.2 |
| `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.2 | 0.3.0 |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.1 | 0.2.0 |
| `vta-service` (dev) | 0.13 | 0.14.16 |
| `affinidi-messaging-core` (floor) | 0.1.5 | 0.1.6 |

## The one source change

`affinidi-messaging-core` 0.1.6 marks `Protocol` `#[non_exhaustive]` and adds a
`DIDCommV1` variant (Aries RFC 0019), so the inbound dispatcher's `match` in
`openvtc-core/src/didcomm.rs` no longer compiles as written.

It gains a wildcard arm that logs and drops. That is the correct handling, not a
placeholder: OpenVTC speaks DIDComm v2.1 and TSP, neither listener it installs
ever negotiates v1, and nothing downstream of that match could read a v1
payload. The arm is also what keeps the *next* variant from being a compile
break.

The core floor moves to 0.1.6 to match. This is load-bearing rather than
cosmetic — on 0.1.5 the enum has neither the attribute nor the variant, so the
wildcard is an unreachable pattern and `-D warnings` rejects it. I checked
0.1.4/0.1.5/0.1.6 sources directly rather than assuming.

Everything else rode the bump untouched — the join ceremony, the reciprocal VMC
exchange, and the TSP leg all dispatch on `vta_sdk::protocols` constants rather
than string literals. That indirection is why this is mostly a lockfile change
and not an audit of every dispatch site.

## `deny.toml`: two ignores removed

RUSTSEC-2026-0215 (`smallstr` unmaintained) and RUSTSEC-2024-0370
(`proc-macro-error` unmaintained). Both crates left the graph with this refresh —
verified against the lockfile, not just inferred from `cargo deny`'s
unmatched-ignore warning — exactly as each ignore's comment predicted. The
remaining ignores still match and stay.

## Pins that survive re-evaluation

`rand` 0.8 and `x25519-dalek` 2.x stay. `pgp` 0.20.0 is still the latest release
and its manifest still declares `rand ^0.8.6` / `x25519-dalek ^2.0.1`; I read the
published manifest rather than trusting the existing comment. Comment date
refreshed to record the re-check.

`generic-array` and `matchit` remain behind latest — both transitively pinned by
other crates, not reachable from our manifests.

## Known duplicate, upstream to fix

`did-git-sign` 0.4.1 still depends on `vta-sdk` 0.19.28, so the binary links two
vta-sdk majors. That belongs to `verifiable-git-infrastructure`, not here — per
CLAUDE.md, protocol/infra changes target that repo. Recorded in the CHANGELOG so
it is not silently carried.

## Verified

- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo deny check` — advisories, bans, licenses, sources all ok
- `cargo test --workspace --all-features` — **640 passed, 0 failed**
- `cargo test --workspace --all-features -- --ignored` — **13 passed, 0 failed**.
  These are the ones that actually exercise the bumped crates: the in-process
  mediator transport round-trip, the join/self-remove lifecycle, and the MockVta
  bootstrap against `vta-service` 0.14.
- Builds check under default, `--all-features`, and `--no-default-features`.

## Pre-merge checklist

```
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*)
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*)
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1)
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers
```

Checklist note, honestly: this PR adds no outbound client, no retry loop, no lock
scope and no mutation — the only source change is a drop arm in an existing
inbound dispatch loop, which is a `continue` in a loop that already survived
unparseable frames the same way. The boxes are ticked as "unchanged and still
true", not as new work verified.

title: chore(deps): hard-pin the enforced-authcrypt TDK and refresh the lockfile
body:
Supersedes #900.

## Why #900 could not be rebased

#900 was authored on 6 Aug against a main that has since moved. **#902 already
landed the substance of it**: the direct `affinidi-messaging-sdk` pins in
`vta-sdk` / `vta-service` / `tests/e2e` are on `0.19`, and the
`UnpackMetadata` `#[non_exhaustive]` test helper in `vti-common` is fixed
(with a better comment than #900 carried). Rebasing #900 would resolve to a
diff of one manifest line plus a stale lockfile, and its three version bumps
(`vti-common` 0.11.35, `vta-sdk` 0.21.7, `vta-service` 0.14.11) are all
already claimed on main by other PRs. Its changelog fragment filename also
collides with `changelog.d/900-envelope-type-from-the-binding-crate.md`.

This PR carries forward what was genuinely left, and finishes the job.

## The pin

`affinidi-tdk = "0.8"` accepted any 0.8.x. The enforced-authcrypt fix
(affinidi-tdk-rs #671) — `unpack` rejecting plaintext / anoncrypt /
forged-`from` envelopes **by default** — first ships in **0.8.5**, through
`affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.19 + `affinidi-messaging-didcomm` 0.15.8.

The lockfile happened to hold 0.8.5, so the property held *by accident*. A
`cargo update`, a lockfile regeneration, or a clean checkout resolving afresh
could each move sender authentication back out of the library, and nothing
would flag it. The requirement now states what the code depends on, with the
reason recorded at the pin.

Defence in depth is unchanged: `bind_authcrypt_sender` and the DIDComm
`inbound_gate` still enforce this above the library.

## A dead workspace dependency

`affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service` is removed from
`[workspace.dependencies]`. No member consumes it — it is absent from
`Cargo.lock` entirely, and `vta-service` and `vtc-service` both carry comments
recording that they replaced it with local `shim.rs` / `router.rs`
equivalents. #900 proposed bumping it to `0.3.22`; that would have been inert.
A requirement that resolves nothing is worse than no requirement, because it
reads as a supported edge.

## Lockfile refresh

`cargo update` collapses two long-standing duplicate trees:

- **`affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.18.65 is gone.** It survived behind
  `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` → `affinidi-messaging-mediator` — the
  dev-only e2e / `vtc-service` fixture chain #902 explicitly called out as
  still carrying a 0.18 copy. `test-mediator` 0.2.47 moved to sdk 0.19, and
  `mediator` 0.18.9 with it. The graph now holds **one** messaging SDK.
- **The legacy `ssi-*` stack drops out** — `ssi-jwk`, `ssi-jws`,
  `ssi-dids-core`, `ssi-json-ld` and ~15 siblings — taking `reqwest` 0.11,
  `sha2` 0.9, `ripemd160`, `tiny-keccak`, `uint` and `windows-sys` 0.48 with
  it. `reqwest` unifies on 0.13.4.

Net **−1393** lockfile lines.

`curve25519-dalek` (5) and `ed25519-dalek` (3) stay single, as #887 / #889 /
#890 left them. `elliptic-curve`, `ecdsa`, `p256` and `sha2` remain doubled
across the RustCrypto 0.13 → 0.14 transition — still upstream-gated, not
something this PR can close.

## Scope

Manifest + lockfile only. No workspace crate's source changes, so no version
bumps and nothing to publish.

## Verified

- `cargo check --workspace --locked` on 1.97
- `cargo check --workspace --locked` on **MSRV 1.95.0**
- `cargo clippy --workspace --locked -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace --locked`
- `scripts/check-lockfile-self-pins.sh` — no workspace crate pulled from crates.io

title: DTG Core Credentials now cites this framework normatively for its taskContext binding (pinned to existing mechanisms; one small optional ask)
body:
# DTG Core Credentials now cites this framework normatively for its `taskContext` binding (pinned to existing mechanisms; one small optional ask)

## Context

[trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#11](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/11) flagged that DTG Core Credentials placed normative requirements on `taskContext`-bearing credentials (outcome evidence, terminal states, etc.) that depended on "the planned DTG Core Trust Task Protocols specification" — which doesn't exist yet, so the requirements were untestable.

Resolution ([dtgwg-cred-spec#15](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/15)) restructures that section to depend only on mechanisms **already defined in this framework's current editor's draft**, rather than on any future spec:

- **Terminal state** = presence of a `#response`-variant document ([§4.4.1](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#441-request-and-response-variants)) or a `trust-task-error` document ([§8](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#8-error-responses)), correlated by `threadId` ([§4.9](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#49-the-threadid-member)).
- **Outcome integrity** = the existing per-specification `proof`-required declaration ([§7.3 item 8](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#73-specification-requirements)).
- **Outcome artifact structure** = the existing per-specification `#response` payload schema ([§7.3 item 7.6](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#73-specification-requirements)).
- **Evidence discovery / retrieval authorization / confidentiality** — sidestepped for cred-spec's v1.0 by requiring the outcome document to travel *with* the credential presentation, rather than be discovered/retrieved asynchronously by a verifier who wasn't party to the original exchange. (This framework's bilateral, transport-bound request/response model doesn't naturally support that kind of later, third-party retrieval, so cred-spec isn't relying on it.)

cred-spec now requires that any Trust Task specification a VTC/VTN designates as the referent of a DTG credential's `taskContext` — a "qualifying" specification — declare `proof` REQUIRED on its response/error variants and define a `#response` schema (or rely on `trust-task-error`). That's it; no framework behavior change required for this to work.

**No action needed on your side for cred-spec's fix to land.** Filing this mainly so you're aware of the cross-reference (per the coordination cred-spec's Governance Considerations already calls for between the two task forces), and to flag one small, genuinely optional framework enhancement that would make part of this more robust.

## Optional ask: let a Trust Task specification declare `threadId` as REQUIRED-and-unique

cred-spec needs `taskContext` (its own name for a `threadId`) to reliably name *one specific* exchange. Right now `threadId` is framework-wide `MAY`, and [§4.9](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#49-the-threadid-member) is explicit that it "carries no normative validation semantics" — no presence guarantee, no uniqueness guarantee, and consumers can't reject on it.

cred-spec works around this by putting the uniqueness burden entirely on DTG *issuers* (its own conformance target), which is sufficient for cred-spec's purposes but means the framework's own consumer-side machinery can't enforce it — a misbehaving issuer's threadId reuse isn't independently rejectable the way, say, a missing required `proof` is (`proofRequired`, [§7.2 item 7](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#72-consumer-requirements)).

Proposal: add a declarable property to [§7.3](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#73-specification-requirements), mirroring item 8's Proof requirement pattern:

> **Thread requirement** — an explicit statement of whether `threadId` is OPTIONAL or REQUIRED for documents implementing the specification, together (where REQUIRED) with the uniqueness scope it MUST satisfy (e.g., "unique per exchange instance for the life of the specification's use"). A conforming consumer MUST reject a document lacking a REQUIRED `threadId` with `malformedRequest`, consistent with the existing `recipient`-required pattern ([§7.2 item 5](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#72-consumer-requirements)).

This is additive only — it doesn't touch `threadId`'s existing general-purpose, loosely-specified behavior for specifications that don't opt in. It would let a future DTG-ceremony Trust Task specification (or any other specification with the same need) get framework-level enforcement instead of relying on the depending spec's issuer-side discipline alone.

Happy to draft this as a PR here if it's wanted, or to help co-author a worked-example Trust Task specification for a DTG ceremony (e.g. relationship witnessing) satisfying the "qualifying" profile above, as a joint appendix in either repo — similar in spirit to your own Appendix A. Let us know which is useful.

title: feat(bindings): draft the DIDComm v1 binding specification
body:
`trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` shipped in #187 without a binding specification to
implement, leaving the carriage and identity rules stated only in Rust doc
comments. This writes them down.

Written **from** the working implementation rather than ahead of it, so the open
questions are concrete, and structured to mirror `bindings/didcomm/0.2` section
for section — a reader who knows the v2.1 binding can diff them.

## What v1 forces that v2.1 did not

**No envelope type of its own.** It rides Aries `basic-message`, whose type has
two interchangeable document URIs. Credo emits the `https://didcomm.org` one by
default, so §1 requires consumers to treat them as equivalent and **forbids**
comparing `@type` by string equality — which silently drops conforming peers.

**Carriage had to be chosen.** v2.1 puts the document in `body`; v1 has none, and
RFC 0095 types `content` as a display string. §2 specifies an `~attach` decorator
under the reserved id `trust-task`; §2.1 records the alternatives and why not.

**Attribution takes a step more, normatively.** A v2.1 envelope authenticates a
DID. A v1 envelope carries **no DID at all** — a bare verkey, with the
verkey→DID binding held as connection state. §3 enumerates three outcomes rather
than two, and requires consumers to distinguish *"nobody authenticated this"*
from *"somebody did and we cannot name them"*. The second is a missing connection
record on the receiving side; collapsing them hides an operational fault behind
what looks like a hostile message.

**Threading needs the wire value, not the defaulted one.** §3.1 maps `thid`/`pthid`
per SPEC §9.1 and requires comparison against the `thid` *as it appeared on the
wire*. RFC 0008 defaults an absent `thid` to the message `@id`, a different
identifier space from the document's `id`, so comparing the defaulted value
manufactures disagreements out of conforming messages.

## Open questions are marked as such

§2 carries an explicit ⚠ flag — including whether `basic-message` is the right
carrier at all. Its assumed advantage is reach, but a consumer needs a handler
under *every* option considered, and v1 mediator forwarding is type-agnostic, so
a dedicated `@type` would route just as well and mirror `binding/didcomm/0.1`
more closely. Nothing depends on the choice yet, so it stays cheap to change.

The Status section says plainly that this is a starting point for the DTG Core
Credentials task force to amend — useful to any reader, not just them, since it
marks what is settled and what isn't.

## Also

One row of the error mapping now matches what the crate actually does: anoncrypt
and unbound-verkey both yield `proofRequired` where the consumer has any means of
replying. I'd written the spec saying "no framework code applies" while the crate
mapped both to `proofRequired` — a contradiction worth catching before anyone
implemented against it.

Crate docs now cite the binding rather than describing it as forthcoming.

## Verification

Registry clean (288 specs, 405 example documents) · `cargo test --workspace` 31
suites · clippy clean · binding serves alongside the others
(`didcomm didcomm-v1 https push tsp`).

Refs #173

title: fix: don't wipe the generated tree on bad input, and make the receipt composable
body:
Two problems found while adding `vtc/relationships/request` in #190.

## 1. Codegen deleted before it validated

`clean_generated_tree` ran *before* the generate loop, so a spec that failed to
generate left the tree wiped. A malformed `payload.invalid-examples.json` — I
wrote `why` where the schema wants `note` — deleted **335 files**, left the
workspace uncompilable, and surfaced only as a later `cargo fmt` error about an
unresolvable `mod acl`, pointing nowhere near the file at fault.

`generate_one` no longer writes: it returns the path and contents, `main`
collects every module, and only once all have generated does the clean run and
the writes happen.

Verified by reintroducing the same bad input:

```
Error: failed to generate code for vtc/relationships/request/0.1
Caused by: …/payload.invalid-examples.json[0].note must be a string

modules before: 26      modules after: 26      outstanding diff: 0
```

The error now names the file, and the tree is untouched.

## 2. The shared issuance receipt couldn't be composed

#189 *documented* that `vta/credentials/issue` restates `IssuedCredential` inline
because the shared definition sets `additionalProperties: false`, which under
`allOf` rejects `supersedes` and `ext`. With breaking changes on the table that's
fixable rather than merely explainable.

**The obvious fix doesn't work, and a test caught it before it shipped.** Simply
swapping `additionalProperties` for `unevaluatedProperties` on the shared
definition still fails:

```
  ok   shared members only              -> true
  FAIL + supersedes                     -> false
  FAIL + ext                            -> false
```

`unevaluatedProperties` inside a *referenced* subschema sees only what that
subschema evaluated, so it rejects the composing schema's members exactly as
`additionalProperties` did. Only a closure at the **outer** level sees everything
the composition matched.

So `credentials/_shared/0.2` splits the two roles:

| | |
|---|---|
| `IssuedCredentialBase` | the members, deliberately **open**, for composition |
| `IssuedCredential` | `allOf` over the base + `unevaluatedProperties: false` — a drop-in closed shape for standalone use |

`vta/credentials/issue/0.2` composes the base and closes at its own level, so the
receipt is **referenced rather than duplicated**. Per §6.6 item 3, adopting a new
component version needs a new specification version; `0.1` stays for the two
specs still pinned to `_shared/0.1`.

Ajv confirms all seven cases:

```
  ok   shared members only              -> true
  ok   + supersedes                     -> true
  ok   + ext                            -> true
  ok   missing required credential      -> false
  ok   unknown member still rejected    -> false
  ok   closed IssuedCredential accepts valid
  ok   closed IssuedCredential rejects extras
```

typify flattens the composition into a single struct, so the generated Rust is
unchanged in shape.

## Knock-on

- **SPEC §7.3 item 7.4** now accepts `unevaluatedProperties`, *requires* it for
  schemas assembled by `allOf` over a shared component, and says a component
  meant for composition should leave itself open.
- The registry build's closure check accepts either keyword. It previously
  warned on any schema without `additionalProperties` — which would have flagged
  the only construction that actually composes.

## Verification

Registry clean (288 specs, 405 example documents) · `cargo test --workspace` 31
suites · clippy clean · TS 43/43 · smoke passes · infra 14/14 · codegen
idempotent both sides.

No version bump — no library API changed; `credentials/_shared/0.2` and
`vta/credentials/issue/0.2` are registry artifacts, and the generated bindings
gain the new module without altering existing ones.

title: feat(vtc): bring VRC request/issue onto Trust Tasks as relationships/request
body:
Finishes a migration that was already half done. `vtc/relationships/{publish,
list,graph,revoke}` exist; request/issue stayed on the legacy
`https://firstperson.network/vrc/1.0/*` DIDComm types. Promised to @bmiller59 on
#173.

## Three legacy message types → one specification

| legacy | becomes |
|---|---|
| `vrc/1.0/request` (`{reason?}`, 48h) | the request document |
| `vrc/1.0/issued` | its `#response`, carrying the signed `vrc` |
| `vrc/1.0/rejected` (`{reason?}`, by `thid`) | a `trust-task-error` with `vtc/relationships/request:declined` |

**Collapsing the rejection is the point of the migration, not a shortcut.** An
error response is already a Trust Task document — correlated by `threadId`,
validated and signed by the same pipeline, subject to §8.1's routing rules. A
bespoke `rejected` type means a second refusal path for every consumer to
implement and a second place to get that routing wrong. It also inherits §8.2's
`inResponseTo`, so a retained decline names the request it answers, which `thid`
correlation could never do for anyone outside the exchange.

The legacy protocol fixed the request's lifetime at 48 hours in code. That's the
envelope's `expiresAt` (§4.2) — a producer's choice with a consumer obligation to
honour it, rather than a constant baked into a message type.

## First real use of two 0.3 features

Neither contrived; both fit:

**Per-variant proof.** Request and response are REQUIRED for *different* reasons,
and the declaration now says so separately — an unsigned ask to mint a
relationship credential is a social-engineering surface, while the response
delivers a credential the requester retains and later publishes. Both land on
REQUIRED, but a reader can see which threat each addresses. This is the first
spec in the registry using the per-variant form.

**`targetFrameworkVersion: 0.3`** — joins `trust-task-error/0.3` as the only
specs validating against the envelope schema that recognises `parentThreadId`.

## Scope

`request` and `publish` stay separate exchanges, deliberately. `request` obtains
a VRC from its issuer; `publish` lodges one with the community so it appears in
`list` and `graph`. Neither implies the other — a VRC may be held privately, and
a member may publish one obtained by other means.

## Verification

Registry clean (287 specs, 402 example documents) · `cargo test --workspace` 31
suites · clippy clean · TS 43/43 · smoke passes · codegen idempotent both sides.

Generated constants confirm the per-variant declaration reaches the bindings on
both the request and response impls.

## One thing worth a follow-up

`trust-tasks-codegen` **deletes the generated tree before validating its inputs**.
A malformed `payload.invalid-examples.json` in this PR (I used `why` where the
schema wants `note`) left 335 files deleted and the workspace uncompilable, and
the only symptom was a downstream `cargo fmt` error about an unresolvable module
— nothing pointing at the actual file. `git checkout` recovers it, but validating
inputs before touching the tree would turn a confusing failure into a one-line
message. Not fixed here; happy to do it separately.

issuer; `publish` lodges one with the community so it appears in `list` and

may publish one obtained by other means.
