title: docs(spec): define how an exchange is named from outside the framework (§4.9.1)
body:
Unblocks @bmiller59 on #173. Deliberately small and standalone.

## The gap

`threadId` names one exchange and expresses no relationship to any other.
Exchanges nest in practice — a Trust Task run to complete a step of a broader
interaction is still its own exchange, with its own thread — and the framework
doesn't represent that containment.

So anything referring to an exchange **as evidence that an event occurred** has
more than one thread available and no rule for picking. DTG Core Credentials hit
this with `taskContext`: their witnessed exchange nests a ceremony inside a
relationship exchange, and only the ceremony's own `#response` attests the
witnessing. A `taskContext` pointing at the outer thread would have verifiers
collecting evidence of the wrong event.

## The rule

Name the **innermost** exchange whose documents attest the event, by the **`id`
of the document that initiated it**.

The `id` rather than the `threadId` because [§4.3](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#43-the-id-member)
makes it globally unique and non-reusable — which a `threadId` is explicitly
*not* required to be — and §4.9's existing convention already makes every
document in a thread trace back to it. So the anchor is a value the framework
already guarantees, not a new one.

## Why on its own

This was originally scoped with the `parentThreadId` envelope member coming in
framework 0.3. That coupling was wrong:

- The anchoring rule is what actually unblocks a depending specification. The
  parent-thread member is a *navigation* aid — it lets a holder walk outward
  from the inner exchange — and no anchor depends on it.
- It needs no envelope change, so it carries none of 0.3's version cost.
- Keeping them separate means a later change to that member's shape cannot reach
  back into specifications that cite this rule.

cred-spec can write `taskContext` against this today rather than waiting on the
0.3 release.

## Scope

Prose only. No member added, no behaviour changed, no generated output affected.

**No library bump** — nothing in either library's API changed. That's the
versioning policy from #178 doing its job: SPEC revisions and library versions
move for different reasons.

Registry validates clean (285 specs); the changelog anchor resolves to the new
heading.

Refs #173

title: feat(acl): a general update task, and a direction for scope filters
body:
Two gaps in the `acl/*` family, both found while folding a maintainer's private ACL surface onto it (OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#840 phase A). Neither is implementation-specific — the fold is what surfaced them, not what needs them.

## `acl/update/0.1` — the family cannot currently amend an entry

There is no way to say *"same role, different step-up approver"*. `acl/grant` creates and explicitly refuses role changes; `acl/change-role` moves the role and nothing else; `acl/revoke` removes. A maintainer needing to amend a label, scope set, expiry, step-up requirement or approve-authority had to model it as revoke-then-grant — **a window in which the subject holds nothing** — or invent a private task, which is exactly what happened.

Two refusals in it are enforced rather than advisory, and both exist so a reduction in authority cannot be performed by a task that doesn't look like one:

- **A role member is rejected** (`roleChangeNotPermitted`). `change-role` owns that transition because it takes the current role as a compare-and-swap. Role is the one attribute where a lost update between concurrent writers is a *privilege change* rather than a cosmetic one.
- **Narrowing `scopes` is rejected** (`narrowingNotPermitted`), directing the caller to `acl/revoke`. Removing authority is what an auditor most needs to find, and it should appear in exactly one place. Were narrowing expressible here, "withdrew production access" and "corrected a label" would be indistinguishable in the trail.

Members **replace rather than merge**, which keeps *omitted* (leave alone), *explicit null* (clear) and *empty array* (set to nothing) distinguishable — three intentions a merge cannot tell apart, and under which removal isn't expressible at all.

## `direction` on `acl/list` — one scope, two questions

Where scopes are hierarchical, a scope identifier raises two different questions, and `scope` alone answers only the first:

- **Who may act in this scope?** Entries scoped to it *or to an ancestor* — authority reaches down. (`acting-in`, the behaviour when the member is omitted.)
- **What is granted beneath this scope?** Entries at or below it. (`subtree`.)

It's spelled out in the spec because getting it wrong **fails quietly**: a revocation sweep using the `acting-in` reading returns precisely the entries that are *not* the answer — the ancestors, which keep their authority — while omitting every leaf-scoped grant underneath. Short rather than empty, so it reads as a complete answer.

Additive: omitting the member preserves existing behaviour.

## Two notes for the next spec author

Both cost me a debugging cycle here, so they're in the commit message too:

- **`direction` deliberately carries no JSON Schema `default`.** A default makes codegen emit a non-`Option` field, so a document omitting the member deserializes to the default and re-serializes *with* it — breaking the round-trip conformance test. `default` is annotation-only in JSON Schema anyway; the rule belongs in prose.
- **Its description is one paragraph on purpose.** Codegen renders a multi-paragraph description as indented lines inside `/** */`, which rustdoc parses as a Rust code block and tries to compile — `error: unknown start of token: \``. Reasoning belongs in `spec.md`.

`CONVENTIONS.md` gains a table of which task changes what, plus both enforced boundaries.

## Verification

- `npm run validate` — 257 specs (256 before), 46 shared schemas
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` + `cargo fmt --all` — no drift
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — 303 TS modules
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace --all-targets` — 27 binaries, clean
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate` — clean (invalid-example conformance)
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --doc` — clean
- `cargo package -p trust-tasks-rs` / `tsc --noEmit` — clean

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.2.43, `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.2.43.

title: docs: version the libraries by their own API, not the framework's
body:
Settles the versioning contradiction flagged in #176.

## The claim that stopped being true

`trust-tasks-rs/CHANGELOG.md` opened with:

> this project adheres to a `MAJOR.MINOR` versioning scheme that tracks the
> corresponding `SPEC.md` framework version

That broke when #175 moved the framework to **0.3** while the libraries stayed
on **0.2.x**. But the coupling was wrong before that too — the two versions move
for different reasons:

- A framework revision can change the **spec-authoring contract** without
  altering a single generated type. Framework 0.3 did exactly that: side-effect
  and exposure classes changed what a spec must declare, and the document wire
  format was untouched.
- The library can break **its own API** with no framework change at all.

One number was answering two questions, so it answered neither.

## What replaces it

Semver over the library's own API, decoupled from the framework. A document's
framework version is carried by each specification's `targetFrameworkVersion`
(SPEC §7.3 item 3) — that is where a consumer should read it, and it is already
per-spec rather than per-library, which is the right granularity.

Two consequences are documented in CLAUDE.md, where someone will meet them:

**Behavioural breaks count even when the wire format is unchanged.** A spec that
starts declaring `proof` REQUIRED flips `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED`, and a consumer then
rejects documents it used to accept. Nothing in `specs/` changed shape, but the
library broke. #174 shipped precisely this as a patch (0.2.56) — under the
policy now written down it would have been a leading-component bump. Not
renumbering retroactively, but worth naming so the next one is judged correctly.

**Bumping the leading component is a workspace event.** `trust-tasks-https`,
`-didcomm`, `-proof`, `-tsp` and `-capability-client` each pin
`trust-tasks-rs = "0.2"`. Going to `0.3.0` means updating all five and releasing
them in `publish.yml`'s dependency order. This is what stopped me doing it
casually in #176; `cargo check` catches a miss immediately, so the trap is
meeting it mid-release rather than planning for it.

The npm README made the same tracking claim and gets the same restatement, plus
a note that the two libraries keep matching version numbers — so a given pair is
known to come from one registry revision.

## Scope

Documentation only; no code change. Libraries to **0.2.60**.

Verified: registry clean (285 specs), no codegen drift either side,
`tsc --noEmit` clean, 33/33 runtime tests, smoke test passes.

title: fix(ts): emit .js extensions so the package can actually be imported
body:
`import … from "@openvtc/trust-tasks"` fails with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, and
has since **0.2.55**. Found while verifying the #176 release against the
published artifact rather than the source tree.

```
$ npm install @openvtc/trust-tasks@0.2.58
$ node -e "import('@openvtc/trust-tasks')"
Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find module '.../dist/_runtime/index'
```

## Why

The generated `index.ts` re-exported every module with an **extensionless**
relative specifier:

```js
export * as AclGrant_v0_1 from "./acl/grant/0.1/payload";   // ✗ Node cannot resolve
export * as AclGrant_v0_1 from "./acl/grant/0.1/payload.js"; // ✓
```

The package is ESM (`"type": "module"`), and Node requires an explicit
extension on a relative ESM specifier — it does not probe for `.js` the way
CommonJS resolution did.

## Why nothing caught it

- `tsc --noEmit` is clean: TypeScript's `Bundler` moduleResolution accepts the
  extensionless form and emits it **verbatim**.
- `build-ts-bindings drift` only compares generated output against a
  regeneration of itself — it cannot tell that the output is wrong, only that
  it is stable.
- Nothing anywhere imported the built `dist/` from Node.

And it was invisible in practice because the package was **types only** for its
whole life until last week: an `import type` is erased before it reaches Node,
and bundlers tolerate extensionless paths. The #176 consumer pipeline is what
made it fatal — actual runtime code that could not be imported.

Subpath imports (`@openvtc/trust-tasks/acl/grant/0.1/payload`) were always fine;
only the barrel was affected. In TypeScript a `.js` specifier resolves to the
`.ts` source, so the emitted form is correct at both ends.

## The guard

`npm run smoke` builds `dist/`, imports it from Node exactly as a consumer
does, and drives a document through `consumeInbound` to prove the two halves
work together *through the built artifact* — a proofless `acl/grant`, which
#174 made proof-REQUIRED, must come back `proofRequired`. Wired into `ts.yml`.

A type-level check cannot cover this, which is precisely why it shipped four
times.

## Verified

Against a packed tarball installed into a clean project:

```
proofless   -> rejected  proofRequired
with proof  -> handled   .../acl/grant/0.1#response
oracle case -> suppressed identityMismatch
```

Plus: registry clean (285 specs), `tsc --noEmit` clean, 33/33 runtime tests,
bindings idempotent, `cargo test --workspace` clean.

## Also

Corrects the generator's strategy comment, which claimed generated modules
import shared definitions via relative paths. They **inline** them and have no
relative imports at all — `index.ts` is the only file with any, which is why
this bug had exactly one site.

Libraries to 0.2.59. Merging republishes; anyone on 0.2.55–0.2.58 needs this to
use the root import.

title: feat(ts): implement the SPEC §7.2 consumer pipeline for TypeScript
body:
Closes the largest structural gap found in the audit behind #174 and #175: of
the framework's two reference languages, one had no path to a conforming
consumer.

## The gap

`@openvtc/trust-tasks` shipped types only. A TypeScript implementation had to
hand-roll all eight [§7.2](https://trusttasks.org/SPEC#72-consumer-requirements)
rules — expiry, recipient enforcement, the §4.8.1 identity cross-check, proof
handling, audience binding, and the §8.1 rule that **suppresses** a response
under `identityMismatch` when the transport authenticated no sender to safely
address.

That last one is not a detail anyone is likely to reinvent. The in-band
`issuer` is by definition the contested identity, so emitting the obvious error
turns the endpoint into an identity oracle — and on a transport that signs
error responses, compels the consumer to sign a document about a party that did
not take part in the exchange.

## The change

`trust-tasks-ts/src/_runtime/` — the first hand-written code in the package —
mirrors `consume.rs`, `document.rs`, `transport.rs` and `error.rs` check for
check, in the same order, with the same wire messages. It sits beside the
generated tree rather than in a second package so a consumer gets the types and
the checks that make them meaningful from one install, as `trust-tasks-rs`
does; `clean()` in the generator preserves it.

```ts
const outcome = await consumeInbound({
  transport, spec: AclGrant_v0_1.SPEC,
  proofPolicy: { kind: "verify", verify: myVerifier },
  doc, myVid, now: Date.now(), newErrorId: () => crypto.randomUUID(),
  handler: async (accepted, parties) => respondWith(accepted, id, await apply(accepted, parties)),
});

switch (outcome.kind) {
  case "handled":    return send(outcome.response);
  case "rejected":   return send(outcome.error);   // already addressed per §8.1
  case "suppressed": return log(outcome.reason);   // §8.1 — answering would be an oracle
}
```

The three proof policies are the Rust ones, including `rejectIfPresent`, which
refuses a proof-bearing document rather than silently dropping the proof —
dropping it would mislead the producer about the guarantees of the exchange.

## Per-specification policy on every generated module

Items 5b, 7 and 8 turn on declarations that cannot be recovered from a
document: whether `recipient` is REQUIRED, whether `proof` is REQUIRED, and
whether the spec is a bearer spec. Rust reads them from `Payload` associated
constants; TypeScript had no equivalent. The generator now reads the same front
matter and emits `SPEC`, plus `RESPONSE_SPEC` where a response is defined —
carrying the §7.3 item 5 party swap, so a response's `recipient` requirement
tracks the request's *issuer* party.

**Cross-checked against all 556 generated Rust impls: zero disagreements.** The
only two TypeScript entries without a Rust counterpart are `trust-task-error`
0.1 and 0.2, which Rust hand-writes as `ErrorPayload` rather than generating.

## Tests

33 tests mirroring the set in `trust-tasks-rs/src/consume.rs`, so the two
implementations cannot drift into disagreeing about what conforms. Each §7.2
item, the inclusive expiry bound, all three proof policies, the bearer
exemption from audience binding, and both `identityMismatch` paths — routed to
the transport-authenticated sender, and suppressed when there is none.

Two assert on what must *not* reach the wire: the `rejectIfPresent` message
must not name the consumer's configuration (it would let an unauthenticated
probe fingerprint which endpoints lack a verifier), and the `identityMismatch`
message must echo neither identity (§8.1, §10.4).

`npm test` compiles to `.test-build` and runs `node --test` — no test framework
added as a dependency. `@types/node` is scoped to the test tsconfig so the
published build stays platform-neutral. Wired into `ts.yml` as a new job, since
hand-written code is exactly what the drift guard cannot cover.

## Verification

- `npm run build` — clean, 285 specs
- `cargo test --workspace` — 29 suites, no failures; `clippy` clean
- `npm test` — 33/33
- `tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit` — clean
- TS bindings idempotent, and `_runtime/` survives regeneration

## One thing to decide

Libraries go to **0.2.58**. I first tried 0.3.0, since the changelog says the
scheme "tracks the corresponding `SPEC.md` framework version" and #175 moved
SPEC to 0.3 — but five binding crates pin `trust-tasks-rs = "0.2"`, so that is a
workspace-wide release event rather than a version bump. Left at 0.2.58 here,
but **the stated versioning rule and the actual versions now disagree** and it
is worth settling deliberately: either the libraries move to 0.3.x with all
five bindings, or the changelog's claim gets softened.

Note `trust-tasks-rs` itself is unchanged by this PR; it moves only to stay in
step with the npm package per the CLAUDE.md convention.

## Remaining from the audit

Both need decisions that touch #173, where the follow-up comment is now posted:

- **Per-variant proof declaration** — what would let `credential-exchange/present`
  declare `{request: RECOMMENDED, response: REQUIRED}` instead of being forced
  to REQUIRED on both, as #174 had to do.
- **Self-describing error responses** — breaking for `trust-task-error`, so a
  `0.3` version folder. The piece cred-spec actually depends on.

Refs #173

* fix(ts): let the shell expand the test glob, not Node

The `test` script quoted its glob, which hands expansion to Node's `--test`
runner. That support postdates Node 20 — the version `ts.yml` pins — so CI
failed with `Could not find '.test-build/test/**/*.test.js'` while passing

works on every version.

* ci: run every workflow on Node 24

itself, but letting the shell do it needs nothing from the runtime and cannot
regress on an older local Node.

title: fix(didcomm): take the envelope type from the binding crate
body:
A consent request pushed to an approver device was **delivered, acked, and then discarded unread**.

The DIDComm message carried the **task** type (`task-consent/request/0.1`) where the binding requires the **envelope** type (`binding/didcomm/0.1/envelope`) with the `TrustTask` in the body. A conformant peer rejects that — and rejects it *silently*, because "not an envelope" is indistinguishable from "not addressed to me".

The symptom was a week of nothing: the request arrived on the approver's inbox, verified, de-duplicated, and vanished. No prompt, no log, no decision — and the mediator's queued copy already deleted by the ack.

## Why it drifted

The envelope URI was hand-written in **four** places across the workspace, each with a comment explaining it was a local copy *"to avoid taking a dependency on the binding crate for one constant"*. Nothing connected `consent_request.rs` to the binding it was supposed to implement, so it used the task type and no compiler, test, or reviewer caught it.

`trust-tasks-didcomm` is now a real dependency and `trust_tasks_didcomm::ENVELOPE_TYPE` is the single source. The four copies are gone — the crate that defines the wire format defines the constant.

## TSP is deliberately untouched

The envelope is a property of the **DIDComm binding**, not of the task. TSP carries the Trust-Task bytes directly with no wrapper, and `push_one`'s TSP branch (`serde_json::to_vec(doc)` → `send_routed`) was always correct.

Applying the envelope unconditionally would have broken the working transport to fix the broken one. The change is confined to the two DIDComm sites: the mediator buffer and the guaranteed send.

## The test was pinning the defect

`a_resubmit_re_asks_nobody` asserted `message_type == TASK_CONSENT_REQUEST_0_1` — the task type on the wire, which is exactly what a conformant peer refuses. It now asserts the envelope on the message **and** the task type inside the document, which is the real invariant.

That is the second test in this investigation found to be holding a defect in place. Both described what the code did rather than what the binding requires.

## Known remaining — deliberately not swept in

**Same defect, same peer (the plugin), should be fixed together:**

- `push_granted` — `TASK_CONSENT_GRANTED_0_1`
- `maybe_push_step_up` — `STEP_UP_APPROVE_REQUEST_TYPE`. **Step-up approvals to a device are broken identically** and have not been noticed. `push_one`'s comment says it "mirrors `maybe_push_step_up`" — it faithfully mirrored the bug.
- `consent.rs`'s `CONSENT_APPROVE_REQUEST_TYPE` — family needs confirming

**Different peer, must not be swept in:** `webvh_didcomm.rs` sends bare task types (`TASK_DID_REGISTER`, `TASK_DID_DELETE`, `TASK_AGENT_NAME_*`) to the webvh host and **works** — that peer accepts them. Converting it is a cross-repo wire migration requiring the host to accept envelopes first.

**The real prevention** is adopting `pack_trust_task`, so the type cannot be hand-chosen at all. That needs the bridge to accept pre-packed bytes — a transport-layer change deserving its own design.

760 tests pass, clippy clean, all three repo guards pass.

title: feat(framework): permit family-namespaced extended error codes (SPEC §8.5)
body:
Second of the follow-ups from the audit behind #174. Self-contained, and
resolves a live MUST violation plus a silent registry/library disagreement.

## The problem

[§8.5](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#85-extension-by-individual-trust-task-specifications)
required an extended error code's namespace to equal the emitting
specification's slug exactly. That leaves a family-wide failure mode with no
way to be named once — so specifications broke the rule to say something true.

26 `did-management/*` specs declare `did-management:unknown_domain`, a
condition defined for the whole family in
`did-management/_shared/0.1/CONVENTIONS.md`. Every member can reject a request
naming a domain the consumer does not host, and it means the same thing in
each. Per-slug codes would oblige a consumer to enumerate all 26 to recognize
one condition.

Two things made this worse than a paperwork violation:

**Nothing ever checked the rule.** `spec.meta.schema.json` states it in its
`errorCodes[].code` description and validates only the grammar — JSON Schema
cannot compare one property against another. `npm run validate` passed clean
on all 26.

**The registry and the generated library disagreed silently.**
`Payload::extended_code` derives the namespace from `TYPE_URI` — that is its
whole purpose, so "the slug literal cannot drift away from the type's
identity". A `did-management/did/delete` handler therefore emits
`did-management/did/delete:unknown_domain`, which is **not** the code the
registry advertises. A consumer matching the declared code misses it, falls
through §8.5's unrecognized-code rule to `taskFailed`, and loses the specific
meaning. Nothing anywhere reports a problem. The only workaround was
`TrustTaskCode::new_extended` with a hand-written namespace — reintroducing
exactly the drift `extended_code` exists to prevent.

## The change

The namespace may now be the emitting slug **or** a *family namespace* — a
proper path prefix of it (`did-management/did` or `did-management` for
`did-management/did/delete`).

The relaxation is deliberately narrow, and the narrowness is what keeps it
safe:

- Because a family namespace is always a prefix of the emitting slug, a
  consumer can still verify a received code's namespacing against the
  document's `type` alone — no registry lookup.
- A **sibling's** slug remains forbidden. `acl/revoke` shares a prefix with
  `acl/grant` but is not itself one, and that is precisely the confusion the
  original prohibition targeted.
- Additive: every previously conforming code remains conforming, and the 26
  existing declarations become legal without editing them.

## Enforcement

`checkErrorCodeNamespaces()` in the registry build compares each code's
namespace against the slug and its prefixes. Verified both directions:

| case | on slug | result |
|---|---|---|
| `acl/revoke:borrowedCode` | `acl/grant` | **fails** — sibling |
| `acl:familyCode` | `acl/grant` | passes — family prefix |

`Payload::family_code(namespace, local)` makes the family form reachable from
the drift-safe API, checking `namespace` against the slug derived from
`TYPE_URI` rather than taking it on trust, so the §8.5 prefix rule holds by
construction. Five new tests cover each prefix depth, the response-fragment
case, and three rejections — sibling slug, unrelated namespace, and a partial
segment (`ac` is a string prefix of `acl/grant` but names nothing).

## Also

Corrects the SPEC.md header, which still read **0.2** while Appendix B has
documented a **0.3** since the side-effect and exposure classes landed — the
staleness I flagged to @bmiller59 in #173 and said we'd fix. Like the rest of
0.3 this is an authoring-contract change only: the document wire format is
unchanged, so `targetFrameworkVersion` and document validation are unaffected

title: feat(framework): permit family-namespaced extended error codes (SPEC §8.5) (#175)
body:
feat(framework): permit family-namespaced extended error codes (SPEC §8.5) (#175)

§8.5 required the namespace of an extended error `code` to equal the emitting
specification's slug exactly, and forbade "that of a related or referenced
specification". That left a family-wide failure mode with no way to be named
once, and specifications broke the rule anyway to say something true: 26
`did-management/*` specs declare `did-management:unknown_domain`, a condition
defined for the whole family in `did-management/_shared/0.1/CONVENTIONS.md`.
Every member can reject a request naming a domain the consumer does not host,
and the rejection means the same thing in each.

The namespace may now be either the emitting slug (as before) or a *family
namespace* — a proper path prefix of it. The relaxation is deliberately
narrow. Because a family namespace is always a prefix of the emitting slug, a
consumer can still verify a received code's namespacing against the document's
`type` alone, with no registry lookup, and a *sibling's* slug stays forbidden:
it shares a prefix but is not itself one, which is exactly the confusion the
original prohibition was aimed at. Additive — every previously conforming code
remains conforming.

Two enforcement gaps closed alongside it:

- **Nothing ever checked the rule**, in either its old or new form.
  `spec.meta.schema.json` stated it in prose and validated only the grammar,
  because JSON Schema cannot compare `errorCodes[].code` against `slug`.
  `checkErrorCodeNamespaces()` in the registry build compares them, and fails
  on a namespace that is neither the slug nor a prefix of it.

- **The family form was unreachable from the drift-safe API.**
  `Payload::extended_code` derives the namespace from `TYPE_URI`, so a
  `did-management/did/delete` handler emitted
  `did-management/did/delete:unknown_domain` — not the code the registry
  advertises. A consumer matching the declared code missed and fell through
  §8.5's unrecognized-code rule to `taskFailed`, losing the specific meaning
  with nothing reporting a problem. The only alternative was
  `TrustTaskCode::new_extended` with a hand-written namespace, reintroducing
  the drift `extended_code` exists to prevent. `Payload::family_code` checks
  the namespace against the slug derived from `TYPE_URI`, so the prefix rule
  holds by construction.

Also corrects the SPEC.md header, which still read 0.2 while Appendix B had
documented a 0.3 since the side-effect and exposure classes landed. Like the
rest of 0.3 this is an authoring-contract change only — the document wire
format is unchanged, so `targetFrameworkVersion` and document validation are
unaffected and no `_framework/0.3` schema is needed.

Libraries to 0.2.57.

title: fix: require proof where a task acts as the subject, and emit the response types TS was dropping
body:
Two independent defects found while auditing the registry and the generated
libraries against the framework, plus the release housekeeping for both.

Neither is a change to the wire format. Both are cases where the framework
already said the right thing and nothing enforced it.

## 1. Twelve specs let an unsigned request through to a signing oracle

`keys/sign`, `keys/derive-and-sign`, `keys/derive-and-sign-document`,
`audit/list`, `credential-exchange/{issue,present,request}`,
`vtc/auth/admin-session`, `vtc/members/{personhood/assert,renew,rotate-challenge}`
and `webvh/sync/delete` declared `proof` as `OPTIONAL` or `RECOMMENDED`, so
`IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` generated as `false` and `consume_inbound` accepted a
proofless document against a signing oracle, an admin-session mint, a
credential presented in the subject's name, and an irreversible DID deletion.

Every one of them declares `exposure.actsAsSubject: true`,
`exposure.discloses: secret`, or `sideEffects.level: destructive`.

**Why nothing caught it.** [§7.3 item 8](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#73-specification-requirements)
requires a declaration "no weaker than the default applicable under §4.7.1",
but that constraint cannot be checked as written: §4.7.1's default is a
function of the *transport* — MAY omit over an authenticated channel, SHOULD
otherwise, MUST where the document will be relied on by third parties — and a
specification does not know its transport at authoring time.

`checkProofFloor` in `scripts/build-registry.mjs` derives the floor from the
declarations a spec *does* make, which is the only signal available
statically. This does not conflict with the side-effect and exposure classes
being descriptive rather than prescriptive: that rule forbids deriving a
**consent** requirement from them, and an integrity floor governs how a
document is authenticated, not whether a human must approve it.

Several of the twelve had genuinely considered rationales — that the
`vp_token`'s holder binding, or the OID4VCI key-binding proof, is the proof
that matters and sits inside the body rather than on the envelope. Those
arguments are correct and are **preserved**; each rationale now also states
why the envelope proof is required for a different reason, and names the
threat model item 8 asks for.

⚠️ **Behavioural change.** A document previously accepted without a `proof` is
now rejected with `proofRequired`, and because §7.2 item 8 then applies,
producers must also carry an in-band `recipient` — none of the twelve is a
bearer specification. All twelve are `draft`, where
[§5.2](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#52-compatibility-rules)
permits schema and prose to change in place without notice, so no new version
folders were minted.

## 2. TypeScript was missing the response half of the framework

273 specs declare a `$defs.Response` reachable via the `response` anchor. The
TS bindings exposed an interface for **8**. Nothing `$ref`s `$defs.Response` —
§4.4.1 addresses it out-of-band through the anchor — and
`json-schema-to-typescript` emits only what it can reach from the root, so the
response half of nearly every request/response task was pruned. Rust emits all
273, so the two languages disagreed about what the framework offers.

Fixed with a synthetic reachability probe, compiled in **one** pass and then
stripped. One pass rather than two matters: the compiler de-duplicates
same-named distinct types by appending a counter (`Ext`, `Ext1`, …), and
independent passes number those counters independently, so a name minted in a
response pass could denote a different shape than the identical name in the
request pass.

Two smaller fixes ride along:

- `RESPONSE_TYPE_URI` is now emitted only when the spec defines a response.
  The generator's own comment claimed this; the code never checked. All 285
  specs got it, including the 12 fire-and-forget ones whose consumers §4.4.1
  says **MUST NOT** emit a `#response` document, and `trust-task-error`, for
  which the value is meaningless (§4.4.1 rule 4). The published package was
  handing implementers a ready-made constant for a conformance violation.

- Every module now exports stable `Payload` / `Response` aliases. Emitted
  interface names derive from each schema's `title` (`ACLGrantPayload`,
  `KeysSignPayload`, …), so no name was reliable across specs and generic code
  was impossible. The published README's example was already written against
  `.Payload` / `.Response` and **did not compile**; it does now, with its field
  names corrected.

## 3. Housekeeping

Both libraries to 0.2.56, `Cargo.lock` refreshed, changelog entry added.

`trust-tasks-rs/CHANGELOG.md` carried the `0.2.55` entry twice, verbatim, with
a *different* `0.2.54` beneath each — residue of the #170/#171 version
collision the `0.2.55` entry itself describes. Merged into one `0.2.54` holding
both PRs' content. **Worth a look** in case the real release history differs
from what I inferred from the entries.

Also corrected: a `Payload::extended_code` doc that described the extended-code
local part as lowercase-only (interior uppercase is accepted, and §4.10 item 4
prefers lowerCamelCase); a test comment claiming capitals violate the grammar
when only a leading capital does; a comment in `consume.rs` that narrated the
author reasoning toward the test, including a reversal mid-paragraph, alongside
a discarded fixture; and two CLAUDE.md claims that CI does not guard the
category taxonomy or TS binding drift, both of which it now does.

## Verification

- `npm run build` — clean, 285 specs validated
- `cargo test --workspace` — 29 suites, no failures
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `npx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit` — clean
- Both generators confirmed **idempotent** (regenerating produces no further diff), so `codegen-drift` and `bindings-drift` should pass
- The README example compiled against the real bindings

## Not in this PR

Four items from the same audit need framework changes and should be reviewed
alongside the #173 proposal rather than ride along here:

- **§8.5 category namespaces.** 26 specs declare `did-management:unknown_domain`
  — a *category* namespace where §8.5 says **MUST** be the slug. It is not
  sloppiness: the code is defined once in a category-wide `CONVENTIONS.md` and
  §8.5 gives no way to express that. Nothing validates the rule, and
  `Payload::extended_code` cannot mint the declared code, so registry and
  library disagree silently.
- **Self-describing error responses** (#173 proposal item 2).
- **Per-variant proof declaration** (#173 proposal item 3) — now load-bearing
  for us too: it is what would let `credential-exchange/present` declare
  `{request: RECOMMENDED, response: REQUIRED}` instead of being forced to
  REQUIRED on both.
- **A TypeScript `consumeInbound`.** The package is types-only; TS implementers
  hand-roll all eight §7.2 rules.

Refs #173

title: fix: require proof where a task acts as the subject, and emit the response types TS was dropping (#174)
body:
fix: require proof where a task acts as the subject, and emit the response types TS was dropping (#174)

* fix(codegen): emit the response payload type TS was dropping for 265 specs

273 specifications declare a `$defs.Response` reachable via the `response`
anchor; the TypeScript bindings exposed an interface for 8 of them. Nothing
in the schema `$ref`s `$defs.Response` — SPEC.md §4.4.1 addresses it
out-of-band through the anchor — and json-schema-to-typescript emits only
what it can reach from the root, so the response half of nearly every
request/response task was pruned. The Rust bindings emit all 273, so the
two languages disagreed about what the framework even offers.

Fixed by injecting a synthetic property that makes `$defs.Response`
reachable, compiling once, then stripping the probe. One pass rather than
two is load-bearing: the compiler de-duplicates same-named distinct types
by appending a counter (`Ext`, `Ext1`, …), and independent passes number
those counters independently, so a name minted in a response pass could
denote a different shape than the identical name in the request pass.
Where `$defs.Response` is a bare alias for an external definition the probe
points at that target directly — routing through the local alias splices the
foreign subschema into this document's context and its own internal refs
then resolve against the wrong document.

Also in this commit:

- `RESPONSE_TYPE_URI` is now emitted only when the spec defines a response.
  The generator's own comment claimed this; the code never checked. All 285
  specs got the constant, including the 12 fire-and-forget ones whose
  consumers §4.4.1 says MUST NOT emit a `#response` document, and
  `trust-task-error`, for which the value is meaningless (§4.4.1 rule 4).

- Every module now exports stable `Payload` / `Response` aliases. The
  emitted interface names come from each schema's `title`
  (`ACLGrantPayload`, `KeysSignPayload`, …), so there was no name a consumer
  could rely on across specs and no way to write code generic over a Trust
  Task. The published README's usage example was already written against
  `.Payload` / `.Response` and did not compile; it does now, and its field
  names are corrected to match the actual payload.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* fix(specs): require proof where a task acts as the subject or destroys state

Twelve specifications that exercise the subject's own authority, release
secret material, or cause an irreversible effect declared `proof` as
OPTIONAL or RECOMMENDED. `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` therefore generated as `false`
and `consume_inbound` accepted a proofless document against a signing
oracle (`keys/sign`, `keys/derive-and-sign`,
`keys/derive-and-sign-document`), an admin-session mint
(`vtc/auth/admin-session`), a credential presentation made in the subject's
name (`credential-exchange/{issue,present,request}`), a personhood
assertion and membership re-issuance (`vtc/members/{personhood/assert,
renew,rotate-challenge}`), an audit-tail read (`audit/list`), and an
irreversible DID deletion (`webvh/sync/delete`). An unauthenticated request
to any of those is a forgery vector.

SPEC §7.3 item 8 already required a declaration no weaker than the §4.7.1
default, but that can never be checked as written: §4.7.1's default is a
function of the transport (MAY omit over an authenticated channel, SHOULD
otherwise, MUST where the document will be relied on by third parties), and
a specification does not know its transport at authoring time. So nothing
ever enforced it.

`checkProofFloor` derives the floor from the declarations a spec does make —
`sideEffects.level: destructive`, `exposure.discloses: secret`, or
`exposure.actsAsSubject: true` now require
`proofRequirement.requirement: REQUIRED` — and fails the build otherwise.
This does not conflict with the side-effect and exposure classes being
descriptive rather than prescriptive: that rule forbids deriving a *consent*
requirement from them, and an integrity floor governs how a document is
authenticated, not whether a human must approve it.

Several of the twelve had considered rationales arguing that an envelope
proof adds nothing over an inner proof — the `vp_token`'s holder binding,
the OID4VCI key-binding proof, a VP over a challenge. Those arguments are
correct as far as they go and are preserved; each rationale now also states
why the envelope proof is required for a different reason, and names the
threat model §7.3 item 8 asks for.

This is a behavioural change for consumers of these specs: a document
previously accepted without a proof is now rejected with `proofRequired`,
and because §7.2 item 8 then applies, producers must also carry an in-band
`recipient` (none of the twelve is a bearer specification). All twelve are
`draft`, where SPEC §5.2 permits schema and prose to change in place
without notice, so no new version folders were minted.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore: bump libraries to 0.2.56, and correct stale documentation

Release housekeeping for the two preceding commits, plus documentation that
had drifted from the code it describes.

- `trust-tasks-rs` and `@openvtc/trust-tasks` to 0.2.56; `Cargo.lock`
  refreshed; changelog entry added.

- `trust-tasks-rs/CHANGELOG.md` carried the `0.2.55` entry twice, verbatim,
  with a *different* `0.2.54` entry beneath each — the residue of the
  #170/#171 version collision that the `0.2.55` entry itself describes.
  Merged into one `0.2.54` holding both PRs' content, and one `0.2.55`.

- `Payload::extended_code`'s doc described the local part of an extended
  error code as lowercase-only. `validate_local` accepts interior
  uppercase, as it must: SPEC §4.10 item 4 prefers lowerCamelCase locals
  and only the first character is required to be lowercase. The
  accompanying test comment claimed capitals violate the grammar when only

- `consume.rs`'s suppression test carried a comment that narrated the

body:
Two editorial corrections raised in WG review. Both are
presentation-only: no normative text, schema, or example payload
changes.

Credential ordering (resolves #4). Within the existing functional
categories, the credential types now read [VRC, VMC] [VIC] [VPC,
VWC, VEC]. VRC precedes VMC because it is the simpler credential
and is the order the two are covered in section 7. VEC moves last
because it is more extensible than VWC and leads directly into
reputation.

  to match. The subsection content is untouched; that part of the
  diff is a pure block move.

Document status (resolves #5). The Working Draft number is distinct
from the specification version and increments each time a set of
changes is significant enough to warrant a new WG review.

title: Add the Working Draft number 01
body:
The Working Draft version (second line after the title) is _different_ than the specification version (first line after the title).

The specification version is V1.0. So the second line reads (correctly):

> _Version:_ 1.0

This will remain constant until the final Working Draft of this version of the specification is approved as a **Working Group Approved Deliverable**. Any new version of the spec after that must have a new specification version number.

For their part, Working Draft versions are **two-digit numbers** incremented with each new Working Draft, starting with 01. So the third line should read:

> _Document Status:_ Working Draft 01

Note that it is not required to change the Working Draft number with every single revision. Rather it should change each time a set of changes are significant enough (in the opinion of the editors) to trigger a new review of the changes by other WG members.

title: Adjusting order in DTG credentials in Mermaid diagram in section 4 (and in section 9)
body:
From a narrative standpoint, I recommend this order (left-to-right within the existing categories) in the Mermaid diagram in section 4: [VRCs, VMCs] [VICs] [VPCs, VWCs, VECs]. My rationale for this slight adjustment:

1. VRCs are the simplest DTG credential, so put them before VMCs (which is the order the two are covered in section 7).
2. VWCs are less extensible than VECs — and VECs take use directly into reputation. So put VECs last (which would also adjust the order in section 9).

title: Resolve normative dependency on unpublished Trust Task model
body:
Closes #11.

Narrows [Trust Task Context Binding](spec/body.md) to depend only on Trust Tasks framework mechanisms already defined in its current editor's draft (request/response correlation, error responses, per-spec proof requirement) rather than on the unpublished DTG Core Trust Task Protocols specification.

## Changes

- Adds a **Qualifying Trust Task Specifications** profile: any governance body designating the Trust Task specification behind a `taskContext` value must pick one declaring `proof` REQUIRED and defining a `#response` schema (or relying on `trust-task-error`).
- Precisely defines "matching trust task outcome evidence" in terms of existing Trust Tasks framework document types (§4.4.1, §8).
- Requires outcome evidence to travel *with* the presentation rather than be discovered/retrieved by the verifier — eliminates the evidence-discovery / retrieval-authorization / confidentiality gaps the issue raised, since there's no longer a separate retrieval channel.
- Requires `taskContext` values be unique per issuer, independent of (and stronger than) the Trust Tasks framework's own `threadId` semantics.
- Fixes the stale "neither has been published" framing in Related Specifications; pins the normative reference to a specific Trust Tasks revision.

Renders cleanly via `npm run render`; no other files affected.

title: Require VWC digest to bind the credential to a specific edge
body:
Require VWC digest to bind the credential to a specific edge

The VWC's only REQUIRED fields were `issuer` (the witness),
`taskContext` (a threadId), and `credentialSubject.id` (the observed
party). None of these identify which edge was witnessed: the
counterparty, the relationship, either directional VRC, and the
precise proposition being attested were all left to `digest`, which
was OPTIONAL. A conforming VWC could therefore attest only that some
activity involving the subject occurred during a trust task, not that
a specific relationship edge was established.

Promote `digest` from OPTIONAL to REQUIRED. A required digest pins the
exact VRC the witness is attesting to; a verifier holding that VRC can
recover both relationship endpoints from its `issuer` and
`credentialSubject.id`, satisfying the edge-binding requirement
without adding new fields. This reuses the digest/canonicalization
mechanism just hardened in #7 rather than inventing a parallel one.

Also make explicit that the binding is only as strong as the
verifier's access to the referenced VRC: a digest without the VRC to
hand is an opaque hash, not an identified edge. Reworded the
digest-integrity security consideration accordingly, and added a
paragraph to the VWC section spelling out what `credentialSubject.id`
+ `taskContext` do and don't establish on their own.

No changes to `witnessContext` (remains OPTIONAL) or to the worked
example, which already populated `digest`.

Closes #10

title: feat(delivery): see what a Guaranteed send actually did
body:
A durable send that never reached its mediator was **indistinguishable from one that arrived**.

`send_guaranteed` returns the moment the outbox entry is written, and the three delivery loops that move it afterwards (`drain_loop`, `outbox_drain_loop`, `confirmation_loop`) logged nothing. So the whole state machine — `Queued → Sent → Delivered | Unconfirmed | Failed` — ran in silence, and a send settling `Unconfirmed` after its `deliver_by` elapsed produced no output at all.

## Why this exists

Diagnosing a live *"the approver is never notified"* report reached a dead end: the sender logged a correct push (#898 — right approver, right mediator, right transport), the recipient's inbox was confirmed listening on the right DID, and the message still never appeared.

Establishing that it had **never reached the mediator** required hand-SHA256'ing DIDs to match the mediator's hashed recipient records against the VTA's plaintext ones. That is not a diagnostic path anyone should have to find.

## What changed

**`VtiOutboxStore::put` logs every transition.** It is the single point every state change passes through, so one log site covers the entire lifecycle. `Unconfirmed` and `Failed` are `warn` — the send is over without confirmed delivery — and the rest are `info`. Spotting a message that never arrived shouldn't require knowing the state machine.

Each line carries `dest_hash = sha256(dest_did)` beside the plaintext DID. The mediator records recipients as hashed DIDs, so this is the field that makes a sender log line greppable against a mediator one — replacing the manual hashing above.

**`send_guaranteed` stops discarding the message id.** It was bound as `_msg_id`, leaving nothing to correlate a send against: not the outbox entry, not the mediator's record, not the recipient's. It now logs `msg_id`, recipient, type, `deliver_by` and idempotency key **before** the enqueue, so an enqueue that fails still names what was being sent and to whom.

## Expiry — deliberately unchanged

Neither transport carries a message expiry, and that stays true:

- DIDComm `expires_time` is not set. Per the existing comment in `send_guaranteed`, `deliver_by` bounds the outbox **hop-retry** window, not content validity — a held push must remain collectable until the request's own `expiresAt`, and a shorter transport expiry could make the mediator drop it before an offline device reconnects.
- The **TSP envelope has no expiry field at all** (verified against `affinidi-tsp` 0.1.13).

So consent expiry is application-level: `task-consent/request/0.1` carries `expiresAt`, and the executor holds the authoritative `PENDING_TTL_SECS`. Anything consuming a queued push must check the payload, not the transport.

## Scope

Instrumentation only. No behaviour change, no wire types, no config — same sends, same recipients, same delivery semantics. The difference is that the outcome is now on the record.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide §9)

```
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*)
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*)
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1)
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers
```

**R6.\*** is the whole PR, and both halves apply:

- *Background-job failures are surfaced* — a Guaranteed send settling `Unconfirmed` is precisely the background failure the rule means, and it was silent. It is now a `warn`.
- *Claim only what was verified* — the `warn` says "settled without confirmed delivery", not "failed": `Unconfirmed` means no end-to-end evidence was obtained, which is not the same as knowing it was lost. The wording preserves that distinction rather than overstating it.

**R1.1** is worth noting as the underlying rule: this makes the difference between "handed to transport" and "delivered" observable, which is the evidence the rule demands and which the sender previously could not produce.

title: fix(consent): say when an approver is not notified
body:
A consent request the VTA decides **not** to push produced no output on a normal deployment. The skip was `tracing::debug!`, so at INFO the log showed a perfectly healthy sequence — `pending:raised`, requests minted and signed, a 422 back to the caller — with nothing indicating that no device had been told.

From the outside that is indistinguishable from a device that is simply asleep, and the two have opposite fixes: a config error on the VTA, versus a client that needs to reconnect.

This is not hypothetical. Diagnosing a live "the browser extension never pops up" report came down to guessing between those two for several rounds of log-passing, because the one line that decides it was compiled to a level nobody runs in production.

## What changed

**The no-route skip is now `warn`**, and says what it means: the approver learns of this request only if the *requester* relays it — which a CLI cannot do to a browser extension. It also reports the configured mediator, since a `did:key` approver routes via the VTA's own `[messaging] mediator_did` and an unset one is the likeliest cause.

**A successful push logs at `info`** with the approver DID, the mediator, and the transport. This was previously unanswerable from a normal log: the approver DID appeared *nowhere*, so an approver-set entry naming a stale device DID looked identical to a working push.

The push log is emitted **before** the enqueue rather than after. The enqueue is the last thing this service controls; beyond it the message is the mediator's to hold and the device's to collect, and silence there is not ours to claim in either direction. What must be on the record is that we tried, to which DID, over which mediator — so a missing prompt can be attributed to a side rather than argued about.

## Deliberately not changed

`push_granted`'s equivalent skip stays at `debug`. That notice is explicitly best-effort and non-load-bearing — the requester re-submits regardless and the single-use grant is the real gate — so a lost one costs a poll cycle, not an approval. Raising it adds noise without adding a decision anyone acts on.

## Scope

Observability only. Same requests, to the same approvers, by the same routes. No wire types, no config, no control flow beyond the log statements themselves. Full `vta-service` suite and `clippy --all-targets` clean; all three repo guards pass.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide §9)

```
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*)
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*)
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1)
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers
```

**R6.\*** is the entire point of the PR, and both halves of the rule apply:

- *Background-job failures are surfaced* — a silently-skipped notification is exactly the failure the rule means. It is now surfaced.
- *Claim only what was verified* — which is why the success log sits before the enqueue and says "pushing", not "delivered". The VTA cannot verify the device received anything, so it does not say so. Moving the line after a successful enqueue would have been the easy mistake: it would read as delivery confirmation for something that is only a hop-accepted handoff.

One lock note against R1.3: the config read guard is now scoped to a block and dropped before the route decision and any send, rather than being held across the `await`s that follow.

title: Specify both VMC directions so membership requires member consent
body:
The spec asserted in five places that two VMCs form a complete membership edge, but the normative schema required `issuer` to be the VTC/VTN C-DID and the subject to be the member, making the reverse credential unconstructible. Issue #8 correctly flagged this as a structural contradiction rather than an editorial one.

The pair is deliberate: the member-issued VMC is the member's consent artifact. A community can always issue a credential naming someone as a member, but it cannot produce the acknowledgement without that party's signature, so requiring both directions makes an unconsented membership claim unprovable. That rationale appeared nowhere in the text, which is why the contradiction was reachable in the first place.

So the prose was right and the schema was the defect. The two directions are now distinguished by issuer and subject rules rather than by a new credential type, matching how the VIC's two variants are handled.

- `spec/body.md`: VMC schema gains direction-qualified issuer/subject rules and a `digest` binding the acknowledgement to the grant, reusing the existing VWC digest algorithm verbatim; a second worked example; a new "Membership Edge Completion" subsection carrying the completeness, ordering and verifier rules plus the consent rationale; and a lifecycle editor's note deferring revocation to the planned Trust Task Protocols spec.
- `spec/body.md`: the per-direction witnessing rule generalised from VRCs to both edge-credential subtypes, so a witnessed membership edge has a defined `credentialSubject.id` binding.
- `spec/body.md`: new Security Consideration for unconsented membership assertion; "Digest integrity" extended to cover the VMC acknowledgement digest.
- `spec/terms-definitions/`: seven files corrected, including the "always ... C-DID" clause in `verifiable_membership_credential.md` that was the term-level source of the contradiction, and the CTA being "automatically" made a member without acknowledging.
- `CONTEXT.md`: VMC entry rewritten to describe both directions.

The verifier rule is deliberately direction-sensitive, which is the part worth reviewing closely: a member presenting their own community-issued VMC is accepted alone, since the act of presenting is itself the consent. A blanket "both always" would have broken the Community-Anchored ZKP and PHC constructions, which rely on the member holding only the community-issued half.

Resolves #8

title: Resolve the contradiction in VMC bidirectionality
body:
## Summary

The specification describes membership as a bidirectional graph edge formed by two Verifiable Membership Credentials, one in each direction. However, the normative VMC schema appears to permit only a community or network C-DID to issue a VMC to a member.

Under the current issuer and subject rules, it is not clear how the reverse-direction credential could be created.

## Detail

The specification indicates that:

* two VMCs, one in each direction, form a complete membership edge;
* the VMC issuer is the VTC or VTN C-DID; and
* the VMC subject is the member’s M-DID, or a VTC C-DID in the network-membership case.

A credential issued by the member to the community would therefore appear to violate the normative issuer rule.

This creates a structural inconsistency in the membership model rather than only an editorial ambiguity. Implementers cannot determine whether membership is:

* a unilateral community-issued assertion;
* a mutually issued credential pair;
* a community assertion plus member acceptance;
* or another form of bidirectional protocol state.

## Requested clarification

Please clarify what constitutes the reverse direction of the membership edge and specify the applicable issuer, subject and validation rules.

One possible resolution would be to model a VMC as a unilateral, community-issued membership assertion that creates a directed graph edge, while representing member acceptance or possession separately at the protocol or presentation layer.

Alternatively, if two credentials are required, the second credential and its semantics should be defined explicitly.

title: feat(cli): a CLI can answer a consent gate instead of dying on it
body:
A `requireConsent` rule made the task it gates unreachable from the command line. `pnm` printed

```
✗ Protocol error: trust task failed [taskFailed]: task failed: auth:consent_required
```

and exited. No digest, no instruction, no way forward — so an operator whose policy gates `webvh/dids/update` could not manage those DIDs from the CLI **at all**, however privileged. The browser extension implemented the approval loop; nothing in Rust did.

A consent refusal is not a dead end. It is a question the VTA is holding an answer for, and everything needed to answer it was already on the wire — the SDK was throwing it away.

## The refusal is now actionable

`trust_task_error` folded every rejection into `VtaError::Protocol(String)`, discarding `details`. `VtaError::ConsentRequired` now carries `payload_digest`, `challenge`, `approver_set`, `min_approvals`, `exclude_requester`.

Detection keys on `details.reason` — where the gate deliberately puts the machine-readable answer, so consumers don't key on the top-level `code` (`taskFailed` for every gated task) or the free-text message.

## `excludeRequester` is now reported

The gate knew whether the requesting device may approve its own request, and didn't say. Without it a CLI must blind-attempt a self-approval and read `denied:requester_excluded` back — so it can't tell the operator whether to approve *here* or on *another device*, the one thing they need to know.

This reveals policy shape to a caller that has already authenticated and just triggered the rule. It grants nothing; the gate still decides every approval. The SDK defaults it to `true` when absent, so an older server yields "use another device" — correct wherever a second device exists.

## Waiting, without turning a refusal into a nag

`vta_cli_common::consent::with_consent` wraps a submit and waits. Shared with the offline `vta` binary so both CLIs behave identically.

There is no read-only status surface for task-consent, so "approved yet?" can only be asked by submitting again — and whether that's safe depends on state in a way that's easy to get wrong:

- **Pending** — the gate recognises the payload, returns the *same* `challenge`, and deliberately does not re-notify. The push follows the question, not the submit. Polling cannot ring the approver's device.
- **Denied or lapsed** — the pending record is **deleted**. The next submit finds nothing, raises a *new* question, and pushes again.

So the loop stops the instant the challenge changes. Continuing would convert a "no" into repeated prompts — the habituation attack the gate's own notes call out, where a prompt an attacker can summon on demand is worth more than one they must wait for. One re-prompt after a denial is unavoidable without a server-side status task; an unbounded stream is not.

The timeout is bounded because an operator is at a terminal, and giving up isn't failure: the request stays pending, so re-running resumes on the same challenge.

Retries clone the body rather than rebuilding it — the grant is bound to a payload digest, so a request that differs on retry raises a second unanswerable question instead of consuming the approval in flight.

## Testing

Five loop cases: approval lets the task through; an ungated task submits exactly once; **a changed challenge stops the loop** (asserting the call count, so a regression that keeps polling fails); the wait is bounded; a non-consent error propagates rather than reading as "still waiting".

Three SDK cases built from the gate's real rejection shape: the refusal carries what answering needs; an absent `excludeRequester` defaults to the restrictive reading; a non-consent failure carrying a `details` object stays a `Protocol` error, so the new variant can't swallow unrelated rejections.

**One trap worth flagging for review**: the SDK tests need `--features client`. The module is feature-gated, so without it they compile out and pass vacuously — `--lib` alone reported an unchanged 239 and looked green. That's the third time in this series a test has looked like coverage without being it, so I checked the count moved (305) rather than trusting the pass.

## Scope

Remote approval only — the CLI shows the code and waits for a device. This is what works with a `exclude_requester = true` two-device policy.

Letting the CLI approve its **own** request needs a `task-consent/decision/0.1` signer, which exists in no client crate. That's the single-operator posture (`exclude_requester = false` with the CLI's DID in the approver set) and is deliberately not in this PR — it's real crypto, not a flag.

Deliberately **not** done: making `exclude_requester` per-requester-DID. That would turn a structural second-device control into a per-identity opt-out, granted to the admin CLI — the highest-value identity to compromise. Both postures are already expressible per deployment; only the client half was missing.

Wired into `did-mgmt dids edit`; the helper is generic and other gated commands can adopt it.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide §9)

```
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*)
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*)
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1)
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers
```

- **R1.4** is the substantive one. The poll is bounded in both duration and continuation: fixed interval, hard deadline, and a terminal stop on a changed challenge. The re-submit is idempotent *by server design* while pending (same payload → same challenge → no re-notify), which is exactly why it is safe to repeat and why it must stop when that stops holding.
- **R1.5** — a non-consent error terminates rather than being swallowed as "keep waiting"; pinned by test.
- **R3.\*** — `excludeRequester` is camelCase, additive, and optional on intake. Read defensively (`unwrap_or(true)`) so an older server degrades to the safe reading rather than a wrong one.
- **R5.\*** — the absent-field default is the restrictive one.
- No new HTTP clients, no config surface, no mutations.
